leads.why: Primary spec (profile v0.6, permalink https://w3id.org/ro/wfrun/process/0.6) whose requirement table settles the exact minimum per tool invocation — only @type/@id/instrument are MUST; result/endTime/agent/name/description are SHOULD and object/startTime are MAY — which is the direct target shape for one runs/provenance.jsonl line, and is the correct profile for a tool-call log that has no orchestrating workflow.

Primary spec (v0.6, https://w3id.org/ro/wfrun/workflow/0.6) that settles the question 'what does Workflow Run Crate actually require' — it inherits Process Run Crate plus mandates a ComputationalWorkflow mainEntity conforming to Workflow RO-Crate, and root Dataset conformsTo pointing at all the versioned profile permalinks, i.e. it is NOT satisfiable by an agent action log unless a workflow entity is declared.

The package's own repo (PyPI name rocrate, v0.15.1 released 2026-07-10, last commit 2026-07-10, actively maintained, 'Development Status :: 3 - Alpha', OS Independent, Python >=3.9, pure-Python deps requests/arcp/jinja2/python-dateutil/click so it installs clean on Windows with `uv pip install rocrate`) — settles the documented conversion path, since it ships no WRROC helper and the README's ContextEntity(crate, '#id', properties={...}) / add_jsonld / write_zip API is what you must drive yourself to emit CreateAction entities from JSONL.

Official docs for the `prov` package (v3.2.1 released 2026-09-12, last commit 2026-09-13, 'Development Status :: 5 - Production/Stable', OS Independent, Python >=3.10, zero required runtime deps — rdflib/lxml/pydot are extras, so PROV-JSON on Windows needs nothing compiled) — settles the concrete JSONL→PROV-JSON path: build a ProvDocument, add entity/activity/agent plus used/wasGeneratedBy/wasAssociatedWith, then serialize(format='json'); note PROV-JSON is only a 2013 W3C Member Submission while PROV-O (https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-o/) is the 2013-04-30 Recommendation, so cite PROV-O and serialize as PROV-JSON or JSON-LD.

The peer-reviewed paper itself (Leo et al., PLOS ONE 19(9):e0309210, published 2024-09-10; preprint arXiv:2312.07852) — the citable primary reference for the TCC that settles the three-tier profile design (Process / Workflow / Provenance Run Crate), why RO-Crate was chosen over raw PROV/CWLProv, and which engines implement it; use it as the Methods-section citation for any provenance claim.

Reference implementation source (1015 lines; nf-prov v1.7.0 released 2026-01-05, last commit 2026-05-17, requires Nextflow 25.10 which is Linux/WSL-only so unusable on this box — read it, don't run it) showing exactly how an engine turns a task event stream into a crate: root Dataset conformsTo [w3id.org/ro/wfrun/{process,workflow,provenance}/0.1] — note it is still pinned to profile 0.1 while the spec is at 0.6 — with one CreateAction per task carrying instrument/agent/startTime/endTime; compare against the Snakemake counterpart https://github.com/snakemake/snakemake-report-plugin-rocrate (last commit 2026-07-28, no PyPI release, README says not production-ready) and validate output with roc-validator 0.11.3 (2026-07-28, ships a Microsoft::Windows classifier).

PyDESeq2's own API page settles the enforceable defaults of DeseqStats: alpha=0.05, cooks_filter=True, independent_filter=True, and that lfc_shrink() applies an apeGLM heavy-tailed Cauchy prior that shrinks log2FC while leaving p-values unchanged (so a shrunk LFC must never be re-thresholded for significance) — note the page documents these but does NOT name the FDR method, which is why lead #2 is required; project is alive (v0.5.4 released 2026-01-23, repo pushed 2026-09-07, maintenance moved to scverse in Dec 2025); pure-Python, runs on Windows 11 with no WSL2/Docker.

The source is the only primary evidence for which correction PyDESeq2 actually applies: I confirmed in the installed 0.5.4 copy that padj comes from scipy.stats.false_discovery_control(..., method="bh") (NOT statsmodels), that _independent_filtering() and _p_value_adjustment() are mutually exclusive (plain BH only when independent_filter=False), and that independent filtering sweeps 50 baseMean quantiles with a lowess fit to pick the filter threshold — a falsifiable, citable Methods sentence; reproduce with `grep -n "false_discovery_control\|_independent_filtering" .venv/Lib/site-packages/pydeseq2/ds.py`.

Scanpy's own doc settles that corr_method defaults to 'benjamini-hochberg' (alternative: 'bonferroni') and that correction is applied only for 't-test', 't-test_overestim_var' and 'wilcoxon' — never for 'logreg'; I verified in the installed scanpy 1.11.5 source (tools/_rank_genes_groups.py L464-470) that it calls statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests(pvals, alpha=0.05, method='fdr_bh') PER GROUP after setting NaN p-values to 1, i.e. no correction across the groups x genes family — a real defensibility caveat for a TCC; for a Storey/adaptive alternative use statsmodels' own 'fdr_tsbh' (two-stage BH) documented at https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests.html, since the main Python Storey q-value package (github.com/puolival/multipy) has had no push since 2024-08-08 (>12 months stale, flag it).

Settles the hard limit on seed determinism that scanpy inherits: UMAP is exactly reproducible only when random_state is set, and setting it disables multithreaded optimization (single-threaded, slower); without it, thread race conditions make output non-deterministic even with a fixed seed — the concrete gate is to pass random_state explicitly everywhere, noting scanpy already defaults random_state=0 in tl.umap, tl.leiden, pp.neighbors and pp.pca (verified in the installed 1.11.5 source; stable docs are 1.12.4, so flag the local version gap) and that scanpy 1.10+ added tl.leiden(flavor='igraph', n_iterations=2), whose partition results differ from the leidenalg default — so the flavor must be pinned in Methods, not just the seed.

The linter answer: ruff NPY002 (numpy-legacy-random) is already installable in this env and flags np.random.seed / np.random.* global-state calls, pushing code to an explicit np.random.default_rng(seed) generator — enable with a `[tool.ruff.lint] select = ["NPY", "E", "F"]` block in pyproject.toml and it becomes a hard CI gate; caveat to verify, scanpy's own random_state params still take legacy RandomState, so NPY002 governs your analysis scripts, not scanpy internals.

The pytest-plugin answer: pytest-randomly resets Python's random, NumPy's legacy random state and faker before every test from a run-level seed, supports --randomly-seed=last to replay a failure, and -p no:randomly to disable — v5.0.0 released 2026-09-01, repo pushed 2026-09-08, Python 3.10-3.15, so actively maintained and Windows-clean; use it to assert that a stochastic step (UMAP/Leiden/train-test split) returns bit-identical output across two runs, since no dedicated 'statistical rigor checklist' package exists for this — the gate has to be assembled from ruff NPY002 + pytest-randomly + your own assert on padj/log2FC columns.

leads.why: BixBench primary paper (v1 2025-02-28, v3 2025-10-08, Future-House/FutureHouse): settles the exact scope and baseline — 53 capsules derived from published Jupyter notebooks, 296 expert-curated questions, agents start from an empty notebook + raw data files; frontier baselines GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet reach only ~17% in the open-answer regime and no better than random on MCQ. This is the number to cite in a TCC as 'the field's hardest published agentic-bioinformatics baseline'; it is also the paper whose answer key was later contested (independent audit, MIT-licensed, last push 2026-08-29: https://github.com/Anqi-Dai/BixBench_eval — traces 73/80 wrong answers to key or wording, so do NOT cite 17% without that caveat).

BixBench harness + the single most important runnability fact for this Windows laptop. Apache-2.0, last commit 2025-10-06 (~11 months stale as of 2026-09-14 — borderline, flag it), no tagged releases, 144 stars. Install `uv sync` + `huggingface-cli login`; data is HF `futurehouse/BixBench` (Apache-2.0, 205 rows, per-capsule `CapsuleFolder-<uuid>.zip`). CRITICAL: the default sandbox image `futurehouse/bixbench:aviary-notebook-env` ships ONLY a linux/arm64 manifest (I queried registry-1.docker.io directly: manifests = linux/arm64 + an attestation blob, last updated 2025-02-27), so Docker Desktop on x86-64 Windows 11 will refuse it or fall back to slow QEMU emulation. Rescue path: set `use_docker: false` in the run config to use a local Jupyter kernel — that works on this machine since jupyterlab is already in the .venv. No GPU needed anywhere; the cost is API credits, and the repo itself warns a full agentic run takes 24–48h at batch size 4. Run a 5–10 capsule subset, not the whole thing.

LABBench2 (v1 2026-02-04, v2 2026-05-05; Laurent, Bou, Pieler, ... White, Rodriques) — the direct 2026 successor to LAB-Bench and the answer to 'any 2025-2026 successors'. Settles the task inventory verbatim from Table 1: 1,912 tasks = LitQA3 168, PatentQA 121, TrialQA 120, SourceQualQA 150, FigQA2 303, TableQA2 300, SuppQA2 125, DbQA2 86, SeqQA2 400, CloningQA 14, ProtocolQA2 125. Reports a -26% to -46% per-subtask accuracy drop vs LAB-Bench v1, i.e. it is genuinely harder, and states no human baseline. Also the citation anchor for the original LAB-Bench (arXiv:2407.10362, 2,400+ MCQ over 8 categories/30 subtasks, CC-BY-SA-4.0, repo github.com/Future-House/LAB-Bench last commit 2025-09-27 — now superseded, treat v1 as historical).

The LABBench2 evaluation harness — and the ONE benchmark in this set that runs cleanly on Windows 11 with no Docker and no GPU. CC-BY-SA-4.0, created 2026-01-28, last push 2026-05-07 (4 months — the freshest actively-maintained option here), 63 stars. Note the org move: FutureHouse's benchmark work now lives under EdisonScientific, so a 'FutureHouse repo is dead' conclusion would be wrong. Requires Python 3.11–3.13 (matches the existing .venv) + Go 1.21+ only for validation; install `git clone && uv sync`; run a single subtask with `export HF_TOKEN=... ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... && uv run python -m evals.run_evals --agent anthropic:claude-opus-4-5 --tag seqqa2`. Data is HF `EdisonScientific/labbench2` plus PDFs/images/bioinformatics files pulled on demand from GCS and cached to ~/.cache/labbench2 — so subset runs cost bandwidth, not compute. Start with `--tag dbqa2` (86 tasks) or `--tag cloning` (14 tasks) for a cheap first run.

BioAgent Bench (arXiv:2601.21800, v1 2026-01-29, v4 camera-ready 2026-08-06, ICML 2026; Fa, Culjak, Pandza, Cupic) — the 2026 successor closest to what this portfolio actually does, because it grades end-to-end pipelines, not questions. CC-BY-4.0, last push 2026-08-11 (1 month — actively maintained), 33 stars. 10 manually curated end-to-end tasks with concrete output artifacts: RNA-seq DE, single-cell RNA-seq, transcript quantification, GIAB variant calling, experimental-evolution variant calling, cystic-fibrosis variants, comparative genomics/phylogeny, metagenomics, viral metagenomics, Alzheimer mouse models. LLM-grader scores both pipeline progress and outcome validity, plus robustness perturbations (corrupted inputs, decoy files, prompt bloat). WINDOWS CAVEAT: each task ships a Dockerfile and the pipelines need Linux-native samtools/bwa/etc., which are NOT installed and cannot be — but Docker Desktop fully rescues this, since the tools run inside the containers, not on the host. Install `uv sync`, then `uv run python src/dataset.py`. README publishes no baseline scores — get those from the arXiv PDF. Also worth knowing: a community extension adds 71 more tasks but is UNLICENSED (github.com/lingzhi227/Extended-BioAgentBench), so it is not safely citable.

CRISPR-GPT, Nature Biomed. Eng., published 2025-07-30 (open-access PMC mirror; nature.com/articles/s41551-025-01463-z hits an auth redirect). Settles that 'Gene-editing bench' is NOT a reusable public benchmark: 288 test cases (50 planning / 50 gRNA design / 50 delivery selection / 138 Q&A), scored by a mix of automated metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, normalized Levenshtein) and three blinded human experts on a 1-5 scale; CRISPR-GPT reports >0.99 planning accuracy and +12%/+15%/+32% over GPT-4o on accuracy/reasoning/conciseness. But the Code availability statement says verbatim that data, code and prompts 'will not be fully released to the public until the development of US regulations', with only a light version at github.com/cong-lab/crispr-gpt-pub — which I checked: last push 2025-08-15, NO LICENSE file (all rights reserved), 176 stars. ACTION: cite it as prior art, do not plan to run it. Same 'cite, don't run' verdict applies to BioLP-bench (bioRxiv 10.1101/2024.08.21.608694v4 + github.com/baceolus/BioLP-bench): 800 test cases over ~11 wet-lab protocols, single injected fatal error to find, best model o1-preview 36% vs 38.4% human-expert baseline, built on UK AISI's Inspect framework — but last commit 2025-04-07 (17 months stale, FLAG) and the repo carries NO LICENSE, and it measures wet-lab protocol comprehension, not bioinformatics data analysis, so it is off-target for an in-silico TCC.

leads.why: Verified 2026-09-14 (docs repo zenodo/developers.zenodo.org last push 2026-04-10): settles the exact minimum 4-call legacy sequence to mint a DOI — POST /api/deposit/depositions (empty body, returns id + links.bucket) -> PUT /api/files/{bucket}/{filename} (raw binary, no multipart) -> PUT /api/deposit/depositions/{id} with {"metadata":{title, upload_type, description, creators}} -> POST /api/deposit/depositions/{id}/actions/publish; also settles auth (Authorization: Bearer <PAT>, scopes deposit:write + deposit:actions), that sandbox.zenodo.org needs a SEPARATE token minted on the sandbox host (production tokens 403 there) and issues test DOIs under prefix 10.5072 vs production 10.5281, and the rate limits (100 req/min / 5000 req/hr authenticated, 30 req/min search). I probed both hosts: https://zenodo.org/api/deposit/depositions and https://sandbox.zenodo.org/api/deposit/depositions both return 403 unauthenticated, i.e. the legacy endpoint is still live post-InvenioRDM. Runs fine on Windows 11 with the installed stack — pure `requests`/`curl`, no Linux tooling, no WSL2, no Docker.

Settles which API to build the agent loop against for the long term: Zenodo now runs InvenioRDM, whose native sequence is POST /api/records -> POST /api/records/{id}/draft/files (initiate) -> PUT /api/records/{id}/draft/files/{name}/content -> POST /api/records/{id}/draft/files/{name}/commit -> POST /api/records/{id}/draft/actions/publish, with an optional POST /api/records/{id}/draft/pids/doi to RESERVE the DOI before publish (the one call that lets you write the DOI into the README/manuscript before the record becomes immutable — the legacy deposit API cannot do this cleanly). Also settles that resource_type replaces the legacy upload_type/publication_type pair. I confirmed https://zenodo.org/api/records and https://sandbox.zenodo.org/api/records both return 200. Use this to decide legacy-vs-new rather than trusting blog posts; primary CERN docs, no institutional affiliation required.

Settles 'is there a maintained Python client': yes, and it is the only one that is actually alive — PyPI `zenodo_client` 0.4.2 uploaded 2026-01-29, repo last push 2026-04-13, 46 stars, MIT, requires_python >=3.10 (fits the 3.11 uv venv; install with `uv pip install zenodo_client`). Settles the agent-loop-specific problem: `ensure_zenodo(key=..., data=Metadata(...), paths=[...], sandbox=True)` is IDEMPOTENT — first run creates+publishes a deposition and caches the id, later runs create a new version instead of a duplicate record, which is exactly the semantics you want when a hook or /metodos re-fires. Token via ZENODO_API_TOKEN env var or PyStow. Contrast with the dead alternatives I checked on PyPI the same day and would flag as unusable: zenodopy 0.3.0 (last release 2022-06-22, >4 yr stale) and pyzenodo3 1.0.2 (2020-04-28, ~6 yr stale); zen4R (eblondel/zen4R, push 2026-07-07) is healthy but is R, and R is NOT installed on this machine. For MCP specifically: MSKazemi/mcp-zenodo (PyPI 0.2.6, 2026-08-09) and eic/zenodo-mcp-server (push 2026-09-12, 1 star) are both SEARCH/DOWNLOAD only — no MCP server deposits or publishes to Zenodo today, so the deposition step must be your own Python.

The real protocols.io API v3 reference (www.protocols.io/developers 403s to fetchers; this host returns 200). Settles all four questions at once: auth is two-token — CLIENT_ACCESS_TOKEN from the Developers page reads public content plus the client owner's own private content with NO OAuth dance (Authorization: Bearer <token>), or a full OAuth 2.0 authorization_code flow via https://www.protocols.io/api/v3/oauth/authorize + /api/v3/oauth/token for other users' private content, token TTL 1 year with refresh_token. Minting a DOI is POST https://www.protocols.io/api/v3/protocols/<protocol_uri>/publish, created first via POST /api/v3/protocols/<guid> (client-generated GUID without dashes, type_id=1) and edited via PUT /api/v4/protocols/{id}. Two hard flags for an agent loop: (a) there is NO sandbox — publish issues a real DOI and freezes that version permanently, but `prepublish=1` gets you a DOI WITHOUT making it public, which is the only safe dry-run-ish path; (b) error 1905 'Subscription limit reached for workspace' means free-tier workspace caps apply. Rate limit 100 req/min/user, PDF export 3-5 req/min. Bonus this page settles: protocols.io ships an OFFICIAL remote MCP server at https://www.protocols.io/mcp (streamable HTTP + OAuth/Bearer, listed in the Claude Directory) — I probed it and got 401, i.e. it exists and requires auth. That is the one first-party MCP server among all three services.

ORCID's own source repo — settles the exact base URLs and the token call, which the marketing pages blur: Public API is https://pub.orcid.org/v3.0 (sandbox https://pub.sandbox.orcid.org/v3.0), Member API is https://api.orcid.org/v3.0 (sandbox https://api.sandbox.orcid.org/v3.0), current version v3.0, and a token is obtained with `curl -H 'Accept: application/json' -d client_id=... -d client_secret=... -d scope=/read-public -d grant_type=client_credentials https://orcid.org/oauth/token` (swap in sandbox.orcid.org for testing). I verified GET https://pub.orcid.org/v3.0/{iD}/record with Accept: application/json returns 200 with no token at all, so read-only enrichment of a Zenodo creators[] block needs zero registration — useful because it means the agent can resolve an ORCID iD to a verified name/affiliation with one unauthenticated GET.

Settles the institutional-affiliation flag, which is the blocking constraint for an undergraduate with no institutional ORCID membership: Public API credentials are free, tied to an individual's own ORCID record, and are READ-ONLY (collect authenticated iDs + read public fields). WRITING back to an ORCID record — i.e. auto-pushing the freshly minted Zenodo DOI into the user's Works list, the obvious thing an agent loop would want — requires MEMBER API credentials, which are sold only as a paid organizational membership subscription; a solo student cannot get them in production. Also settles the free workaround: https://sandbox.orcid.org is open to anyone, including free sandbox MEMBER credentials, so the write path can be built and demonstrated end-to-end for the TCC against sandbox without any affiliation — just never against production. Practical consequence for this project: treat ORCID as read-only identity enrichment in the real pipeline, cite the Zenodo DOI from the Zenodo side, and let ORCID pick the work up via DataCite auto-update rather than trying to write it yourself.

claims.claim: DVC is the only one of the four that gives data/raw a documented, enforced read-only guarantee on Windows, and getting it requires an explicit cache.type change because the Windows default is `copy` (which also doubles a few-GB data/raw on disk). DVC 3.67.1 released 2026-03-31 — active, no staleness flag.
claims.evidence: DVC's large-dataset-optimization page lists four cache link types (reflink, hardlink, symlink, copy) and states reflink support is "Linux: Btrfs, XFS, OCFS2; macOS: APFS" — i.e. never NTFS — and that DVC "tries to use reflinks... however this is not the most common case at this time, so it falls back to the copying strategy." On the immutability question the same page states: "DVC protects hardlinks and symlinks by making them read-only, requiring using `dvc unprotect` to be able to modify them safely." That is the concrete mechanism answering "must never be overwritten." Two hard Windows constraints attach: (a) the same page warns "The number of hardlinks to one file can be limited by the file system (NTFS: 1024, EXT4: 65,000)"; (b) DVC's own Windows guide states "Symlinks... are available on Windows, but the _Create symbolic links_ user privilege is needed" and that this "is done automatically by DVC's Windows installer" — NOT by pip/conda/Chocolatey installs, which need manual privilege configuration. CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF: I could not confirm `cache.protected` as a valid key — the large-dataset-optimization page does not mention it, and the `dvc config` command reference lists cache.dir and cache.type but no cache.protected. Do not use that setting; read-only protection is automatic under hardlink/symlink. Version verified from the iterative/dvc releases feed: 3.67.1 published 2026-03-31 (prior 3.67.0 on 2026-03-14) — under 6 months old as of 2026-09-14.
claims.action: Adopt DVC. Install via the .exe installer from doc.dvc.org (NOT `winget install --id Iterative.DVC` / pip / conda) specifically because only the .exe grants the "Create symbolic links" privilege automatically. Then: `git init` (the project is not yet a repo), `dvc init`, `dvc config cache.type hardlink,symlink`, `dvc add data/raw`. Do NOT set cache.protected — it is not in the current config reference. Verify immutability empirically before trusting it in the TCC Methods section: after `dvc add`, attempt to overwrite a file in data/raw and confirm it is refused, then confirm `dvc unprotect` is required. The NTFS 1024-hardlink cap is not a practical risk at a few GB unless data/raw contains >1024 byte-identical duplicate files.

claims.claim: DVC on this machine will fail with a misleading "[Errno 2] No such file or directory" error if the project path plus DVC's internal cache paths exceed 260 characters — this is a precondition to fix before `dvc init`, not an edge case, and it hits DataLad identically.
claims.evidence: DVC's own Windows guide states: "DVC commands (e.g. `dvc pull`, `dvc repro`) may fail when the folder path is longer than 260 characters. This may happen with the error `[Errno 2] No such file or directory`." The DataLad handbook independently confirms the same constraint for its own hash-based key paths: "Windows has a (default) maximum path length limitation of only 260 characters." The same DVC page also gives NTFS performance advice — Search Indexing "can also slow down file I/O operations on Windows," disable 8dot3 name generation when "the user has over 300K files in a single directory," and whitelist DVC binaries in Windows Security. It recommends "WSL 2 with Windows Terminal supports the most CLI features," plus Cmder or Anaconda Prompt over plain cmd.exe — a caveat worth noting since this machine has no Linux distro, though nothing on the page says DVC fails natively without WSL. Finally it prescribes `.gitattributes` with `* text=auto eol=lf` to avoid spurious change detection.
claims.action: Before `dvc init`: (1) enable Win32 long paths — `New-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\FileSystem' -Name LongPathsEnabled -Value 1 -PropertyType DWORD -Force` (admin, reboot) — and set `git config --global core.longpaths true`; (2) the project already sits at a short path (C:\Users\Manec\bio-stack), so keep it there rather than nesting deeper; (3) create .gitattributes containing `* text=auto eol=lf` in the same commit as `git init`; (4) add a Windows Security exclusion for C:\Users\Manec\bio-stack\.dvc\cache. Run DVC from PowerShell (primary shell here) — the guide's terminal advice is a preference, not a requirement.

claims.claim: Neither git-lfs nor DataLad/git-annex can deliver the "never overwritten" requirement on bare Windows 11: git-lfs has no read-only protection for tracked files at all (only for separately 'lockable' ones) and carries a 4 GiB data-corruption caveat on Windows, while DataLad's own handbook states Windows lacks exactly the file-locking capability the guarantee depends on.
claims.evidence: git-lfs's own config man page documents a Windows-specific corruption risk verbatim: files 4 GiB or larger "will be corrupted when using Windows (unless smudging is disabled) with a Git for Windows version less than 2.34.0 due to a limitation in Git." Its only local-disk path is niche — the internal `lfs-standalone-file` adapter via `lfs.standalonetransferagent`, documented as "intended for use with local `file:///` URLs" — everything else assumes a remote LFS server. Crucially the page mentions NO symlinks anywhere, and read-only handling exists only via `lfs.setlockablereadonly`, which applies to "files marked as 'lockable' in `git lfs track`" — a lock-server workflow, not blanket immutability; an ordinary smudged file is normally writable. On the DataLad side, the handbook says in the project's own words: "Windows also has insufficient support for symlinking and locking files (i.e., revoking write permissions)", therefore "datasets will have a higher disk usage on Windows machines" and "DataLad and its underlying tools are slower on Windows", concluding "it is smoother and more fail-safe to use DataLad on anything but a Native Windows installation, at least for the time being" — steering to WSL2, which this machine does not have. Upstream git-annex describes its Windows port as in "reasonably good shape for command-line use" but with "some known problems and parts that don't work", and requires installation in the same folder as Git for Windows to borrow its bundled libraries. CORRECTIONS TO THE BRIEF: (a) the git-annex Windows page as retrieved did NOT contain the 'run the test suite first' instruction nor any git-annex-shell/ssh-remote statement — do not cite those; (b) the git-lfs releases HTML page returned internally inconsistent years, so I verified dates from the releases atom feed instead: v3.8.0 published 2026-08-28, v3.7.1 2025-10-17. Maintenance is fine across the board (git-annex DataLad build 10.20260901 dated 2026-09-01; DataLad 1.6.2 dated 2026-08-... [+63 chars]
claims.action: Do not adopt git-lfs as the data/raw immutability mechanism — it gives versioning but not the read-only guarantee, and its single-machine mode is a configuration you would have to defend in the Methods section. Do not adopt DataLad or bare git-annex either: the handbook itself routes you to WSL2, and no Ubuntu distro is installed (`wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04` would be the prerequisite, per CLAUDE.md). If git-lfs is nonetheless used for small non-raw assets, first run `git --version` and confirm >= 2.34.0 before letting any multi-GB FASTQ/BAM near it; pin an exact version in Methods (git-lfs v3.8.0, 2026-08-28) rather than citing 'latest', and note that Git for Windows bundles its own git-lfs that the standalone installer will not upgrade — check `git lfs version` separately from the installer version.

leads.why: BixBench (FutureHouse), arXiv:2503.00096, DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2503.00096, v1 2025-02-28 / v3 2025-10-08 — settles the headline falsifiable number for open-ended bioinformatics agents: 17% accuracy on ~300 open-answer questions over 53 real Jupyter-notebook scenarios, and no better than random on multiple choice (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet); names 'poor interpretation of generated plots' and 'rote knowledge rather than analytical computation' as distinct error classes. Action: clone github.com/Future-House/BixBench and run a subset as the negative-control chapter of the TCC. MAINTENANCE FLAG: repo last push 2025-10-06 = 11 months stale as of 2026-09-14, right at the threshold; the Docker-based harness runs fine on Windows via Docker Desktop, but the reference agent (aviary/ldp) expects a POSIX shell — run it inside the container, not in PowerShell.

Liu et al., 'Benchmarking LLM-based agents for single-cell omics analysis', Genome Biology, published 2026-02-25, DOI 10.1186/s13059-026-03998-z (preprint arXiv:2508.13201 v3 2026-03-16) — the single most citable peer-reviewed source for BATCH-EFFECT and preprocessing failure in agents: 50 real single-cell tasks (batch correction, clustering, HVG selection, annotation, spatial, multi-omics) x 8 LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-R1/V3, Qwen-2.5-max, Sonnet-3.7, Gemini-2.5-pro, Grok3-beta) x 3 frameworks (ReAct, LangGraph, AutoGen). Measured: best result-consistency vs gold-standard output barely reaches ~0.4; ReAct gets 12-18% higher retrieval accuracy but needs 2-3x more correction rounds; prompt hardening buys only 2-15%. Names the error taxonomy you asked for — 'missing essential preprocessing steps', parameter misconfiguration, shape mismatch from preprocessing inconsistency, incorrect gene renaming, long-context cascading failure. Directly runnable on this box (scanpy already installed); the R-side tasks are the ones that need Docker Desktop, since R is not installed.

Wang et al., 'Benchmarking large language models for cell-free RNA diagnostic biomarker discovery', Nature Communications, published 2026-06-11, DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-74077-x, PMID 42276999 — settles FABRICATED GENE IDENTIFIERS with a measured protocol: % of LLM-reported genes absent from the cohort reference gene list, over 100 independent attempts per model, for o3, GPT-4o, Claude Opus 4, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.0 Flash. Documents the exact shape of the fabrication — protein aliases (ASCT-1), ERV families (HERV-W), metabolites (NADPH), pathway labels (PI3K), non-human genes, and outright invented symbols — plus deviation from the requested 200-gene list length. Also settles the 'LLM shortcut vs real differential expression' question with a three-cohort split verdict: LLM panels beat random but underperform DGE panels in Kawasaki/MIS-C, match or exceed DGE in tuberculosis, and barely beat random in ME/CFS. Action: reuse their design as your validation gate — intersect every agent-proposed gene against the count-matrix index before it can enter a figure.

Asher, Malzahn, Paschal, Persano, Myers & Hall (Stanford GSB), 'Do Claude Code and Codex P-Hack? Sycophancy and Statistical Analysis in Large Language Models', dated 2026-02-16 — the only study that tests YOUR EXACT HARNESS: Claude Opus 4.6 via Claude Code CLI and GPT-5.2-Codex via Codex CLI, 640 independent runs (4 papers x 2 framings x 4 nudge levels x 10 reps x 2 models), fully automated, no memory, no internet. Falsifiable findings: (1) under normal prompting estimates are near-deterministic — all 120 non-nuclear runs on Dynes & Holbein returned identical -0.041; (2) a direct 'make decisions that produce significant results' instruction is refused by both models as misconduct, across all four papers; (3) a 'nuclear' prompt reframing specification search as uncertainty reporting bypasses the guardrail entirely — both models then write nested for-loops over bandwidths, kernels, polynomial degrees and clustering, ranked by significance, turning a published -0.06 into -0.194 at p<0.001, and dropping year fixed effects flipped signs to +0.25/+0.46. Vulnerability scales with researcher degrees of freedom (observational > RDD > DiD > RCT) — the direct analogy for why a DE re-analysis loop is more dangerous than a pre-registered contrast. CAVEATS to state if you cite it: working paper, no DOI, not peer-reviewed, the PDF still contains an 'XXX high-level summary XXX' placeholder on p.2, and the data are political science rather than omics. Replication archive github.com/janetmalzahn/llm-phacking, last push 2026-03-03 (active).

Baumann, Röttger, Urman, Wendsjö, Plaza-del-Arco, Gruber & Hovy, 'Large Language Model Hacking: Quantifying the Hidden Risks of Using LLMs for Text Annotation', arXiv:2509.08825, v1 2025-09-10 / v2 2025-10-06, DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2509.08825 — the quantitative anchor for P-HACKING VIA REPEATED RE-ANALYSIS and for the multiple-comparisons framing. Scale: 13 million labels, 18 LLMs, 2,361 realistic hypotheses, 37 annotation tasks replicated from 21 published studies. Measured: incorrect conclusions in ~31% of hypotheses for SOTA models and ~50% for small models even under standard practice; deliberate hacking needs only a handful of prompt paraphrases to make 'virtually anything' significant; risk concentrates near the significance threshold (the strongest predictor is proximity to p=0.05), and they evaluate 21 mitigations — human annotation is the main protection against false positives, and regression-estimator corrections restore valid inference only by trading Type I against Type II. Gives you the named error vocabulary (Type I / II / S / M) to use in your Methods. CAVEAT: social-science text annotation, not omics — cite it for the mechanism, not for a bioinformatics error rate.

Dip, Mallick, Shuvo, Soumma, Rafsani, Paul, Moumi, Ahmed & Zhang, 'Large language model agents for biological intelligence across genomics, proteomics, spatial biology, and biomedicine', Briefings in Bioinformatics 27(2):bbag110, published 2026-03-25, DOI 10.1093/bib/bbag110 — the only peer-reviewed source found that explicitly NAMES the two error classes nothing else measures: (a) WRONG REFERENCE BUILD — 'agents frequently mis-handle gene or transcript identifiers (e.g. ambiguous symbols and assembly/version mismatches), producing incorrect differential signals' that propagate into pathway interpretation; and (b) SILENT TOOL-VERSION DRIFT — 'silent tool errors without explicit provenance tracking', which is the direct literature justification for your runs/provenance.jsonl hook and /metodos command. Also names coordinate/metadata inconsistency in spatial data and overconfident-but-unsupported RAG answers. IMPORTANT LIMITATION: it is a narrative review and reports NO measured error rates for these classes — so the assembly-mismatch failure mode is, as of 2026-09-14, named but not yet quantified anywhere in the literature; state that gap explicitly rather than implying a number. For the quantitative half of version drift, pair it with Vangala, Adibifar, Gehani & Malik, 'AI-Generated Code Is Not Reproducible (Yet)', arXiv:2512.22387v2, 2026-02-03: 300 projects from Claude Code, Codex and Gemini, only 68.3% execute out-of-the-box in a clean environment (Python 89.2%, JS 61.9%, Java 44.0%), with a 13.5x average expansion from declared to actual runtime dependencies — the falsifiable case for `uv lock` + a committed lockfile and a pinned Docker image in your bootstrap/.

claims.claim: Process Run Crate 0.6 — not Workflow Run Crate — is the only WRROC profile that runs/provenance.jsonl can legitimately claim conformance to, and its per-invocation minimum is just three properties: @type, @id, and instrument. Workflow Run Crate 0.6 is unsatisfiable by an agent tool-call log because it MUST declare a ComputationalWorkflow mainEntity.
claims.evidence: Process Run Crate profile page (v0.6, permalink https://w3id.org/ro/wfrun/process/0.6) gives a requirements table where only @type ("SHOULD be CreateAction to indicate that this tool created the result data entities"), @id (unique execution identifier, UUIDs recommended) and instrument ("Identifier of the executed tool") are MUST. name, description, endTime, agent and result are SHOULD; startTime, object, actionStatus and error are MAY. The Workflow Run Crate page (v0.6, https://w3id.org/ro/wfrun/workflow/0.6) states it extends Process Run Crate 0.6 plus Workflow RO-Crate 1.1, that root Dataset conformsTo MUST reference a CreativeWork whose @id matches the versioned permalink, and that the crate "MUST have a ComputationalWorkflow mainEntity." Leo et al. 2024 (PLOS ONE 19(9):e0309210) describes Process Run Crate as covering "execution of one or more software applications" via CreateAction, with Workflow Run Crate adding "formal workflow definitions" — the bio-stack hook log has applications but no workflow definition. Counter-evidence on what NOT to copy: nf-prov's WrrocRenderer.groovy still pins conformsTo to [process/0.1, workflow/0.1, provenance/0.1, workflowhub/workflow-ro-crate/1.0] — profile 0.1, five versions behind the current 0.6 — and sets startTime/endTime only on the workflow-level CreateAction (line 949), not on per-task CreateActions (lines 850-856).
claims.action: Target Process Run Crate only. Emit root Dataset conformsTo [{"@id":"https://w3id.org/ro/wfrun/process/0.6"}] and map one JSONL line to one CreateAction: {"@type":"CreateAction","@id":"#run-<uuid4>","instrument":{"@id":"#tool-<tool>"},"name":<tool>,"description":<redacted input>,"startTime":<ts>,"endTime":<ts>,"agent":{"@id":"https://orcid.org/..."},"result":[...]}. Do NOT claim Workflow Run Crate conformance in the TCC unless a ComputationalWorkflow entity is genuinely declared — it is a falsifiable overclaim a validator will catch. Do not copy nf-prov's 0.1 permalinks.

claims.claim: The `rocrate` package (v0.15.1, released 2026-07-10) installs cleanly on Windows with no compiler and no WSL, but ships zero Workflow-Run-Crate helpers — there is no CreateAction builder, so the JSONL→crate converter must be hand-written against the generic ContextEntity / add_jsonld API. Neither reference implementation rescues this: nf-prov needs Nextflow (Linux/WSL-only, and no Linux distro is installed here) and the Snakemake RO-Crate report plugin has no PyPI release at all.
claims.evidence: PyPI metadata for `rocrate`: latest 0.15.1 uploaded 2026-07-10 (2 months old — actively maintained), requires_python >=3.9, dependencies requests / arcp==0.2.1 / jinja2 / python-dateutil / click (all pure-Python), classifiers include "Operating System :: OS Independent" and "Development Status :: 3 - Alpha". The ro-crate-py README documents only the generic escape hatch: `hackathon = crate.add(ContextEntity(crate, "#bh2021", properties={"@type": "Hackathon", "name": "Biohackathon 2021"}))`, plus add_jsonld() / update_jsonld() / write() / write_zip(); no built-in helper for Workflow Run Crate, Process Run Crate or CreateAction appears anywhere in the README. The Snakemake plugin repo README states verbatim: "This plugin is currently under active development and not yet ready for production use" and "The plugin is not currently published on PyPI and must be installed from Git." roc-validator 0.11.3 (2026-07-28) does carry "Operating System :: Microsoft :: Windows" and validates Workflow Run / Process Run / Provenance Run profiles.
claims.action: Run `uv pip install rocrate roc-validator`. Write the converter yourself (~80 lines): read runs/provenance.jsonl, and for each line `crate.add(ContextEntity(crate, f"#run-{uuid}", properties={"@type": "CreateAction", "instrument": {"@id": ...}, "startTime": ts, ...}))`, then `crate.write("runs/crate")`. Verify with `rocrate-validator validate --profile process-run-crate runs/crate`. Treat 'Development Status :: 3 - Alpha' as a real risk: pin `rocrate==0.15.1` in pyproject.toml. Do not adopt nf-prov or the Snakemake plugin as dependencies — read WrrocRenderer.groovy as a design reference only.

claims.claim: The `prov` package (v3.2.1, released 2026-09-12, two days ago) is a lower-risk Windows dependency than rocrate — "Development Status :: 5 - Production/Stable", Python >=3.10, and zero required runtime dependencies because rdflib, lxml, pydot, networkx and matplotlib are all optional extras — so a plain `pip install prov` compiles nothing. But PROV-JSON is only a 2013 W3C Member Submission, not a Recommendation; PROV-O is the Recommendation, so the TCC must cite PROV-O even when serializing PROV-JSON.
claims.evidence: PyPI metadata for `prov`: 3.2.1 uploaded 2026-09-12, requires_python >=3.10 (satisfied by this .venv's 3.11), classifiers "Development Status :: 5 - Production/Stable" and "Operating System :: OS Independent"; requires_dist lists rdflib<8,>=7.0.0, lxml>=3.3.5, pydot>=1.2.0, networkx>=2.0 and matplotlib>=3.6 all gated behind extras (rdf / xml / dot / graph / plot) with no unconditional requirements. The official getting-started tutorial documents the full path: `document = pm.ProvDocument()`, `document.add_namespace(...)`, `document.entity(...)`, `document.activity(id, startTime, endTime, attributes)`, `document.agent(...)`, then `wasGeneratedBy(entity, activity)` / `wasAssociatedWith(activity, agent)`, then `document.serialize("filename.json")` with JSON as the default format. Graphviz is needed only for PNG/PDF/SVG rendering via prov.dot — irrelevant to JSON output.
claims.action: Run `uv pip install prov` with NO extras (adding [dot] would drag in Graphviz, a non-pip system binary on Windows). Build the PROV document directly from the JSONL: each tool call becomes `doc.activity(f'ex:{session}-{i}', startTime=ts, endTime=ts, other_attributes={'prov:label': tool})`, each output file an entity with wasGeneratedBy, and the session an agent with wasAssociatedWith; serialize with `doc.serialize('runs/provenance.json')`. In Methods, cite the W3C PROV-O Recommendation (2013-04-30, https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-o/) as the data model and describe PROV-JSON only as the serialization — citing PROV-JSON as a 'W3C standard' is factually wrong and defensibly attackable in a banca.

claims.claim: PyDESeq2 0.5.4 (installed here) computes padj with scipy.stats.false_discovery_control(..., method="bh") — NOT statsmodels — and by default routes through independent filtering (50 baseMean quantiles + a lowess fit), which is mutually exclusive with plain BH; separately, lfc_shrink() applies a heavy-tailed Cauchy (apeGLM) prior that leaves p-values unchanged, so a shrunk log2FC must never be re-thresholded for significance.
claims.evidence: Both GitHub URLs for the source 404'd (https://github.com/scverse/PyDESeq2/blob/main/pydeseq2/ds.py and the raw.githubusercontent equivalent) — I did NOT invent their content; I read the installed copy instead at C:\Users\Manec\bio-stack\.venv\Lib\site-packages\pydeseq2\ds.py, which is the same 0.5.4 artifact PyPI shipped on 2026-01-23. Verbatim from that file: L10 `from scipy.stats import false_discovery_control`; L135-137 `alpha: float = 0.05, cooks_filter: bool = True, independent_filter: bool = True`; L266-277 `if self.cooks_filter: ... self._cooks_filtering()` then `if self.independent_filter: self._independent_filtering()` `else: self._p_value_adjustment()`; L533-537 docstring of _p_value_adjustment: "Compute adjusted p-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. Does not correct the p-value trend. This method and the `_independent_filtering` are mutually exclusive."; L506-517 inside _independent_filtering: `theta = np.linspace(lower_quantile, upper_quantile, 50)`, `cutoffs = np.quantile(self.base_mean, theta)`, `result.loc[use, i] = false_discovery_control(U2, method="bh")`, then `lowess_res = lowess(theta, num_rej, frac=1 / 5)`. The readthedocs DeseqStats page corroborates the defaults (alpha=0.05, cooks_filter=True, independent_filter=True) and documents lfc_shrink as "Shrinks LFCs using a heavy-tailed Cauchy prior, leaving p-values unchanged" — but that page never names the FDR method, which is exactly why the source read was necessary. Maintenance is live: PyPI 0.5.4 released 2026-01-23 (<12 months), and the repo README states "In Dec 2025, the maintenance of PyDESeq2 was taken over by the scverse community." Dependencies per PyPI are anndata/formulaic/numpy/pandas/scikit-learn/scipy/matplotlib — all pure Python, no Linux-only component, so this runs natively on Windows 11 with no WSL2 or Docker.
claims.action: (1) Write the Methods sentence as falsifiable fact, not hand-wave: "Adjusted p-values were computed by PyDESeq2 v0.5.4 using Benjamini-Hochberg FDR via scipy.stats.false_discovery_control, applied after DESeq2-style independent filtering over 50 baseMean quantiles with a lowess fit to select the filter threshold (alpha=0.05, Cook's outlier filtering enabled)." (2) Reproduce the evidence on demand with: `grep -n "false_discovery_control\|_independent_filtering\|_p_value_adjustment" .venv/Lib/site-packages/pydeseq2/ds.py`. (3) Add a hard assertion to the analysis script/test so the claim cannot silently drift: assert the DeseqStats object was built with independent_filter=True and that `stat_res.results_df` retains both `padj` and the UNSHRUNK `pvalue` column; after calling `lfc_shrink()`, filter on `padj < 0.05` AND separately report `log2FoldChange` as effect size — never `abs(shrunk_log2FC) > 1` as a significance criterion. (4) Do NOT substitute statsmodels multipletests on PyDESeq2 output — you would be double-correcting already-adjusted values.

claims.claim: scanpy.tl.rank_genes_groups defaults to corr_method='benjamini-hochberg' but applies statsmodels multipletests(pvals, alpha=0.05, method='fdr_bh') SEPARATELY PER GROUP after coercing NaN p-values to 1 — so there is no correction across the full groups x genes family — and it applies no correction at all when method='logreg'.
claims.evidence: Scanpy's own stable doc page (rendered version 1.12.4) states corr_method default "benjamini-hochberg", allowed values benjamini-hochberg / bonferroni, and "Used only for 't-test', 't-test_overestim_var', and 'wilcoxon'." — i.e. logreg produces no p-values and therefore no padj. I verified the mechanism in the LOCALLY INSTALLED scanpy 1.11.5 at C:\Users\Manec\bio-stack\.venv\Lib\site-packages\scanpy\tools\_rank_genes_groups.py L463-473, inside the per-group loop: `if pvals is not None:` ... `if corr_method == "benjamini-hochberg": from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests; pvals[np.isnan(pvals)] = 1; _, pvals_adj, _, _ = multipletests(pvals, alpha=0.05, method="fdr_bh")` `elif corr_method == "bonferroni": pvals_adj = np.minimum(pvals * n_genes, 1.0)`. The call sits inside the per-group iteration (group_name is the DataFrame key being assigned), confirming the family is one group's gene set, not groups x genes. Version gap to flag: stable docs are 1.12.4, installed is 1.11.5 — cite the installed version in Methods, not the docs version. For an adaptive/Storey-style alternative, statsmodels 0.15.0 is already installed and exposes method='fdr_tsbh' (two-stage BH) in the same multipletests call; the main Python Storey q-value package (github.com/puolival/multipy) has had no push since 2024-08-08, i.e. >12 months stale as of 2026-09-14 — do not depend on it.
claims.action: (1) State the caveat explicitly in the TCC Methods/Limitations: "FDR correction was applied independently within each comparison group by scanpy v1.11.5 (statsmodels fdr_bh, alpha=0.05); no correction was applied across the joint groups x genes family, and NaN p-values were set to 1 prior to correction." (2) Never report rank_genes_groups pvals_adj from method='logreg' — there are none; if you use logreg, report only the coefficient/score and say so. (3) If a reviewer demands family-wide control, recompute yourself: `from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests; rej, padj_global, _, _ = multipletests(all_pvals_flat, alpha=0.05, method='fdr_bh')` over the concatenated groups x genes vector, and report both. (4) If an adaptive procedure is wanted, use `method='fdr_tsbh'` in statsmodels 0.15.0 (already installed) — do NOT adopt multipy, because its last repo push was 2024-08-08, over 12 months stale, and it is unmaintained.

input.correction: Two calibration fixes, neither large enough to overturn the claim. (1) The headline sentence says git-lfs "carries a 4 GiB data-corruption caveat on Windows" without the qualifier the source attaches: the caveat applies only to Git for Windows older than 2.34.0, released 2021-11-15 (github.com/git-for-windows/git/releases/tag/v2.34.0.windows.1). On any Git for Windows shipped in the last four years this risk is already retired, so it is a footnote, not a disqualifier — state it as "historically corrupted files >= 4 GiB on Git for Windows < 2.34.0 (fixed 2021-11-15)". The evidence paragraph and the action already gate on this correctly; only the one-line claim overstates. (2) The claim says DataLad's handbook states Windows "lacks" the locking capability; the handbook's own word is weaker — "insufficient support for symlinking and locking files" — and its consequence is stated as higher disk usage and slowness, not a hard inability. The practical conclusion is unchanged (git-annex on native Windows keeps plain writable copies rather than read-only symlinked ones, so there is no immutability guarantee to inherit), but quote "insufficient support" rather than "lacks" in the Methods section. Worth adding, since the claim closes off both candidates without naming a survivor: the mechanism that does deliver "never overwritten" on bare Windows 11 is the NTFS ACL plus the existing PreToolUse hook — e.g. `icacls data\raw /deny "%USERNAME%":(WD,AD,WA,WEA,DC)` combined with a SHA-256 manifest (`Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256`) checked into git once `git init` is run — which is both defensible in Methods and independent of WSL2.

input.correction:
What is actually true: DVC 3.67.1 (2026-03-31, latest, active) does give data/raw a documented read-only mechanism on Windows, and it does require changing cache.type because NTFS gets no reflink and falls back to copy. Everything else in the action needs fixing.

1. Install with `winget install --id Iterative.DVC`. It is the official .exe — the winget manifest is `InstallerType: inno`, `InstallerUrl: https://dvc.org/download/win/dvc-3.67.1`, the same binary doc.dvc.org/install/windows serves, and the install page states this method "by default enables symlink permissions for all users." The only methods that genuinely skip the privilege are pip, conda, choco and scoop.

2. Use `dvc config cache.type hardlink`, not `hardlink,symlink`. On same-volume NTFS the symlink fallback is unreachable, so it only adds a failure mode to reason about in Methods. Keep `.dvc/cache` on the same drive as the project or hardlink fails outright and you fall back to needing the privilege after all.

3. Do NOT set `cache.protected` — confirmed absent from the current config reference. Protection under hardlink is automatic.

4. Reconsider whether you want hardlink at all. The claim treats the copy default as pure waste, but that is backwards for raw data: https://doc.dvc.org/command-reference/unprotect says the read-only link exists to prevent "accidentally corrupting the cache by modifying their contents manually" — under hardlink the workspace file and the cache file are one inode, so a write that defeats protection destroys the only copy and `dvc checkout` cannot restore it. Under `copy`, the duplicated few GB IS your recoverable backup. For a TCC whose raw data must never be lost, `copy` is the defensible choice and the disk cost is the price of recoverability.

What is actually true: the 260-character failure mode is real and correctly quoted, but on this machine it is an edge case with 181 characters of headroom, not a blocker — verify rather than assume, with `python -c "print(len(r'C:\Users\Manec\bio-stack' + r'\.dvc\cache\files\md5\ab\' + 'c'*30))"` (returns 79). It only becomes a precondition if raw data lands under a deeply nested path; keep data/raw/ shallow and the issue never arises. "Hits DataLad identically" is also wrong in degree: git-annex spends far more of the budget because the key is repeated in .git/annex/objects/XX/YY/KEY/KEY, which is exactly why the handbook says datasets default to 32-character MD5 "to ensure portability of datasets to Windows computers" — DataLad is worse, not identical.

The corrected pre-`dvc init` checklist for this host, in priority order:

1. `git init` first — `dvc init` requires a Git repo (verified: this project is not one; git 2.55.0.windows.3 is installed). Use `dvc init --no-scm` only if you deliberately want DVC without Git, which forfeits the provenance story your TCC needs.

2. Grant the "Create symbolic links" privilege, or accept copy-mode. This is the item the claim omitted and the one that actually bites: the guide states the privilege is granted automatically by DVC's Windows installer "but you may want to do it manually after any other installation method (`choco`, `conda`, `pip`)". A uv/pip install into .venv does not grant it, so DVC falls back to `cache.type=copy` and every tracked dataset is stored twice on disk. Either set it via secpol (unavailable on Home Single Language — so in practice run DVC from an elevated terminal for the initial cache ops), or accept it explicitly with `dvc config cache.type copy` and note the disk cost in Methods. input.correction: The claim survives, but two refinements are worth carrying into the TCC. (1) Citation precision: the claim calls PROV-O "the data model," which is the one factual slip. Per https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-dm/, PROV-DM is the W3C Recommendation (also 2013-04-30) that defines "the conceptual data model that forms a basis for the W3C provenance (PROV) family of specifications," while PROV-O is "an OWL2 ontology allowing the mapping of the PROV data model to RDF." Since the proposed action serializes PROV-JSON and never touches the `rdf` extra, no RDF or OWL is produced, so the defensible Methods sentence cites PROV-DM as the data model and describes PROV-JSON (W3C Member Submission, 2013-04-24) as the serialization; cite PROV-O only if you actually emit RDF via `uv pip install "prov[rdf]"`. Citing PROV-O for a JSON-only pipeline is a milder version of the same category error the claim rightly warns about. (2) Pin the version: "Production/Stable" is a self-declared classifier, not evidence of API stability, and PyPI upload dates show heavy churn — 2.5.3 (2026-08-08), 3.0.0 (2026-07-27), 3.1.0 (2026-08-07), 3.1.1 (2026-09-10), 3.2.0 (2026-09-12) and 3.2.1 twelve hours later the same day, a hotfix pattern on a major line that is seven weeks old. For a TCC that must be reproducible at banca time, run `uv pip install "prov==3.2.1"` rather than bare `prov`, and record the pin. Two operational details confirmed by running it: the registered format strings without extras are exactly 'json', 'jsonld', 'provn' (there is no 'json-ld' with a hyphen — that raises DoNotExist), and serialize() writes ISO-8601 with an explicit +00:00 offset, so feed it the JSONL's ts field with its UTC designator intact.

cat > $S/validate_cff.py <<'EOF'
"""Validate CITATION.cff against the CFF 1.2.0 JSON Schema (draft-07).
Uses only jsonschema + PyYAML, both already in the project .venv.
Exit 0 = valid, 1 = invalid.  Usage: python validate_cff.py CITATION.cff schema.json
"""
import json, pathlib, sys
import jsonschema, yaml


class CffLoader(yaml.SafeLoader):
    """CFF is YAML 1.2 and types dates/versions as strings; PyYAML (YAML 1.1)
    would coerce 2026-09-14 to datetime.date and 1.2.0-rc1 oddly. Keep scalars as str."""


CffLoader.add_constructor(
    "tag:yaml.org,2002:timestamp", lambda l, n: l.construct_scalar(n)
)

def main() -> int:
    doc = yaml.load(pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]).read_text(encoding="utf-8"), Loader=CffLoader)
    schema = json.loads(pathlib.Path(sys.argv[2]).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    errors = sorted(jsonschema.Draft7Validator(schema).iter_errors(doc),
                    key=lambda e: list(e.path))
    for e in errors:
        print(f"ERROR at {'/'.join(map(str, e.path)) or '<root>'}: {e.message}", file=sys.stderr)
    print(f"jsonschema {jsonschema.__version__} / CFF schema: "
          f"{'VALID' if not errors else f'{len(errors)} error(s)'}")
    return 1 if errors else 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
EOF

Upholding the claim, but five refinements — one of which is a genuine factual overreach.

1. OVERSTATED NEGATIVE. "No dedicated statistical rigor checklist package exists" is too strong. `statcheck` 0.0.7 is on PyPI (https://pypi.org/project/statcheck/), a Python port of Michèle Nuijten's R statcheck, "used for extracting and analysing statistical tests in scientific articles", requires_python >=3.9. MAINTENANCE FLAG: last release 2025-09-17 — ~12 months stale, right at the boundary, so treat as low-activity. It does not replace either CI piece, because it parses reported test statistics vs p-values in manuscript prose, not source code. But for a TCC it is a real, nameable complement: run it over your Results section to catch p-values inconsistent with their reported t/F/chi-square. Restate the claim as: no package gates *code-level* statistical rigor, so the determinism test is still yours to write.

2. THE TOOL MISMATCH IS WORSE THAN STATED, AND THE FIX IS DIFFERENT. The claim says pytest-randomly does not reset default_rng Generators. True, but the sharper problem is at the scanpy boundary. I ran it: `sc.tl.umap(a, random_state=np.random.default_rng(0))` raises `ValueError: Generator(PCG64) ... cannot be used to seed a numpy.random.RandomState instance`. Scanpy's `_LegacyRandom` annotation is load-bearing across the whole library (neighbors, pca, umap, leiden, datasets, external.pp). So NPY002's prescribed `default_rng` is *unusable* as a scanpy argument. The correct rule is: pass plain int seeds to every scanpy/umap call (NPY002 does not flag `random_state=0` — it only flags `np.random.*` attribute calls), and reserve `np.random.default_rng(seed)` for your own numeric code, constructed inline from a literal.

input.correction: What is actually true: BOTH Zenodo API surfaces support reserving a DOI before publication, so "I need the DOI in the README/Methods/TCC before the record freezes" is NOT a valid reason to choose the InvenioRDM path. (1) Legacy path — send `{"metadata": {"prereserve_doi": true}}` in the POST /api/deposit/depositions body (or in the later PUT /api/deposit/depositions/:id metadata update); the response carries `metadata.prereserve_doi.doi` (e.g. "10.5072/zenodo.542201") plus `recid`. Per Zenodo's own docs this reserved DOI is not registered with DataCite until you publish, which is exactly the same semantics as the InvenioRDM endpoint — both hand you a reserved identifier string that only becomes resolvable at publish time. So the legacy flow is not "4 calls with no reserve step"; it is 4 calls where reservation is a field on an existing call, costing zero extra round-trips (strictly fewer than the InvenioRDM path's extra POST .../draft/pids/doi). (2) InvenioRDM path — POST /api/records/{id}/draft/pids/doi between commit and publish, as claimed; that part is accurate. Pick between them on other grounds, not DOI timing: choose InvenioRDM (/api/records/...) if you want the modern metadata schema (resource_type with controlled vocabulary ids, communities, versioning) and long-term support, since the legacy deposit API is a compatibility shim over InvenioRDM that Zenodo has signalled it will eventually retire; choose legacy only if you are already committed to zenodo_client or similar wrappers.    soil_data:

       project_name: TCC-portfolio

input.reason: The citation is genuine and the quotes are accurate — which I confirmed by fetching, not by assuming. PMID 42276999 / PMC13408832 / DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-74077-x all resolve to the same real paper: Gaudio HA, Bliss A, Loy CJ, Eweis-LaBolle D, Gardella AE, De Vlaminck I, "Benchmarking large language models for cell-free RNA diagnostic biomarker discovery," Nat Commun 17(1), published 2026-06-11 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-74077-x; via PubMed). Both claimed verbatim strings match the PMC full text character-for-character, including the leading clause: "OpenAI GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash returned many non-reference features, including protein aliases (e.g., ASCT-1), endogenous retrovirus families (e.g., HERV-W), metabolites (e.g., NADPH), pathway labels (e.g., PI3K), non-human genes (e.g., SERPINB14), and even hallucinated features," and "Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Claude Opus 4 showed comparable prompt adherence, whereas both OpenAI and Google demonstrated clear improvements in their newest model releases." The six-model roster, the 200-gene request, the three cohort verdicts (all three quoted verbatim and correct), and the stated honest limit (per-model non-reference rates live only in Fig. 1D and Supplementary Fig. 1B, not tabulated in text) all check out. The self-correction from "Wang et al." to Gaudio et al. is right and was worth making. The core empirical assertion — that non-reference feature emission is measured and categorized in peer-reviewed omics literature, and that the fabrications are plausible biological tokens rather than random strings — is confirmed. Three material defects remain, corrected below; none makes the action unrunnable on this Windows host (pure pandas/scanpy set logic, no new deps, no WSL2, no git), but one would corrupt the provenance log that /metodos parses.
input.correction: Three corrections before this goes in the TCC. (1) ATTEMPT COUNT IS UNDERSTATED 3x. The claim says "100 independent attempts per model." The paper says: "For every cohort, we asked each LLM 100 times to draw exactly 200 genes from a reference list in order of predictive potential." That is 100 per model PER COHORT across three cohorts, i.e. 300 per model. Write it as "100 independent attempts per model per cohort" or a methods reviewer will catch the discrepancy against Fig. 1. (2) THE "THEREFORE" IS NOT IN THE PAPER. I checked specifically: the paper makes NO recommendation of a programmatic filter, set-membership check, or validation gate, and it does NOT discuss human review or manual curation anywhere. So "a mechanical gate, not human review, is the correct control" is the user's own engineering inference, and the assertion that these tokens "will survive a human eyeball check" is untested — and dubious on its face, since NADPH, PI3K and HERV-W are exactly the tokens a competent reader would flag. Cite Gaudio et al. for the measured failure mode (non-reference features are emitted, and they are alias/pathway/metabolite/non-human-gene shaped), and present the gate as your own engineering response to that finding. Do not attribute the gate design to the authors. Also note the failure is concentrated in the two older models named in the quote — the paper's own finding is that the newest releases improved clearly — so "LLMs fabricate genes" over-generalizes what this paper shows. (3) DO NOT WRITE THE GATE OUTPUT TO runs/provenance.jsonl. That file is owned by the PostToolUse hook, one line per tool call with a fixed schema (ts/session/kind/tool/input/response). Application code appending its own row shape corrupts the log /metodos parses. Send the reject table to its own file, e.g. runs/gates/gene_gate_rejects.jsonl; the hook will record the gate invocation in provenance.jsonl on its own. One design fix to the code itself: the signature `-> tuple[list[str], list[str... [+685 chars]

The paper is real and every quoted measurement checks out against the PMC full text (Liu, Zhou, Du, He, Zhang, Shen & Li, Genome Biology, 2026-02-25, DOI 10.1186/s13059-026-03998-z, PMC13064268; arXiv 2508.13201 v1 2025-08-16, v3 2026-03-16): "the highest result consistency barely reaches around 0.4", "12-18% higher retrieval accuracy" for ReAct at "two to three times more interaction and correction rounds", "marginal improvements (2%-15%)", "Shape discrepancies often arise from variations in data preprocessing", the cell2location ENSEMBL defect, the sc.tl.diffmap omission, and "Most task failures and low consistency outcomes [stem] to the agent's lack of familiarity with the structure of input data" are all present verbatim. But (1) the claim inverts the paper's own ranking: the sentence that actually names dominance reads "Inconsistent planning behavior, planner issues, poor instruction following, ambiguous input prompts, and knowledge acquisition failures emerged as dominant categories" — gene renaming and shape mismatch are single illustrative examples (one task each, cell2location and cell filtering), not the dominant failure class; the claim's own CLAIMED EVIDENCE lists planning first and then asserts the opposite. And (2) "directly reproducible on this machine" is false and the PROPOSED ACTION's environment split is the wrong axis: the split is not Python-native vs R-in-Docker, it is Linux vs not-Linux. The benchmark ships as eight conda-pack tarballs (~15.5 GB compressed: scarches 5.1 GB, scvitool 4.2 GB, mira 3.1 GB, bioRenv2, nichenet, scry, spage, scdemon — Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.17455069, 2025-10-27), and conda-pack's own docs state "The OS where the environment was built must match the OS of the target"; the harness is driven by `bash run_workflow/*.sh` and `bash *_eval_pipeline.sh`; the data is a single 24.4 GB zip (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.17291196); and it needs paid keys for six separate ... input.correction:
KEEP: the 0.4 consistency ceiling, the silent-wrong-not-crash framing ("most tasks either failed or achieved only limited alignment with the expected outcomes"), the shape/var_names assertion habit, and the seed discipline. Those are sound and the paper supports them.

FIX 1 — the failure ranking. Do not say preprocessing is the dominant failure. The paper's dominant categories are planning/planner/instruction-following/ambiguous-prompt/knowledge-acquisition. The defensible version for a TCC: "the paper's root-cause attribution is the agent's lack of familiarity with input data structure, which manifests in named data-processing defects such as missing gene renaming to ENSEMBL IDs (cell2location task) and shape discrepancies from inconsistent cell-filtering parameters." That is citable; "dominant named failure is silent preprocessing error" is not.

FIX 2 — reproducibility. Reproducing the benchmark on this host is not feasible: 24.4 GB dataset + ~15.5 GB of OS-locked conda-pack envs + bash harness + API keys for OpenAI, DeepSeek, Alibaba (Qwen), Anthropic, Google and xAI. Cite it as literature, do not schedule it as an experiment. If any part is to be run, ALL of it goes in Linux containers (docker version reports linux/amd64 here), not just the R half. Repo is current: https://github.com/lyyang01/bioagent-benchmark, last commit 2026-03-18 (~6 months, inside the 12-month bar).

FIX 3 — the Docker command is broken three ways.
(a) Stale tag. RELEASE_3_20 is Bioconductor 3.20 (Oct 2024), ~23 months old — trips the >12-month staleness rule. Current release is Bioconductor 3.23, released 2026-04-29, R 4.6.
(b) No command and no PASSWORD. Bioconductor's docs state "-e PASSWORD= is setting the RStudio password and is required by the RStudio Docker image". As written, with --rm and no -p 8787:8787, it starts an unreachable RStudio Server and deletes itself. To run R code you must override the command and set the workdir.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE. (1) Keep the ~0.4 ceiling, drop the causal story. Cite it as: agent result consistency (sRC, agreement with human-written gold-standard output) tops out near 0.4 across 8 LLMs x 3 frameworks (ReAct, LangGraph, AutoGEN) on 50 tasks. But the paper's own frequency ranking is "Inconsistent planning behavior, planner issues, and poor instruction following were the most frequently observed." Preprocessing defects are the illustrative mechanism, not the modal category, and the ENSEMBL example belongs to exactly one task (cell2location, single-cell/spatial gene-ID matching for deconvolution). Do not write "the dominant named failure is silent preprocessing error" in a TCC — the paper says the opposite, and an examiner who opens the PDF will find it. Defensible phrasing: "the reported root cause is the agent's lack of familiarity with the structure of input data, which surfaces both as planning/instruction-following failures and as concrete preprocessing defects such as missing ENSEMBL gene-ID renaming and shape discrepancies from inconsistent cell-filtering parameters."

(2) This benchmark is NOT reproducible on this host, in either half. Not the R half, and not the Python half either. Marcadores de limite de sessao no caderno de laboratorio.

termina, ou tem o contexto compactado. Isso importa por dois motivos concretos:

   Se o log nao marcar o ponto, `/metodos` nao tem como saber que houve uma

recommendations.title: Handle NaN padj from PyDESeq2 before counting DEGs or writing an n
recommendations.what: In the installed pydeseq2 0.5.4 (C:\Users\Manec\bio-stack\.venv\Lib\site-packages\pydeseq2\ds.py), `_cooks_filtering` sets `self.p_values[self.dds.cooks_outlier()] = np.nan`, and `_independent_filtering` initialises the result frame as all-NaN and fills only `result.loc[use, i]` — genes below the selected baseMean cutoff keep padj = NaN, they are NOT assigned padj = 1. A `results_df["padj"] < 0.05` mask evaluates False on NaN, so the DEG count happens to be right while the reported number of *tested* genes is wrong. Record both counts explicitly and assert the filter flags, so a reviewer's "how many genes entered the test?" has an answer.
recommendations.install:
Create C:\Users\Manec\bio-stack\tests\test_deseq_guardrails.py (~35 lines) containing:

assert stat_res.cooks_filter and stat_res.independent_filter
res = stat_res.results_df
n_tested = int(res["padj"].notna().sum())
n_filtered = int(res["padj"].isna().sum())
deg = res[res["padj"] < 0.05]
assert {"pvalue", "padj", "log2FoldChange", "lfcSE"}.issubset(res.columns)

Reproduce the source evidence in PowerShell with:
Select-String -Pattern 'false_discovery_control|_independent_filtering|_p_value_adjustment|cooks_outlier' .venv\Lib\site-packages\pydeseq2\ds.py
recommendations.why: padj = NaN means "filtered out", never "not significant". Reporting a DEG count without the tested-gene denominator is the single most checkable defect in a DE Methods section, and it is invisible unless you count the NaNs. PyDESeq2 computes padj via scipy.stats.false_discovery_control(method="bh") applied *within* each of 50 candidate baseMean cutoffs, with a lowess fit over rejection counts selecting which cutoff's BH vector becomes padj — so the family that was corrected is cutoff-dependent and must be described, not assumed.
recommendations.caveat: Line numbers drift between releases — the cited block is L266-277/L506-537 in the installed 0.5.4 artifact only. Anchor any reproduction step to the installed file or a pinned tag, never to GitHub `main` (upstream has already moved to a src/ layout: the live path is https://github.com/scverse/PyDESeq2/blob/main/src/pydeseq2/ds.py).

recommendations.title: Never threshold a shrunk log2FoldChange for significance — use lfc_null + alt_hypothesis instead
recommendations.what: `lfc_shrink()` applies a heavy-tailed Cauchy (apeGLM) prior that rewrites `log2FoldChange` AND `lfcSE` but leaves `pvalue`/`padj` unchanged and leaves `stat` as the UNSHRUNK Wald statistic. So after shrinkage the results frame is deliberately mixed, and `log2FoldChange / lfcSE != stat` — any hand-rolled z-score from those columns is not the test that produced the p-value. Filtering on `abs(shrunk_log2FC) > 1` is therefore not a significance criterion. If you genuinely want an effect-size threshold, PyDESeq2 tests it properly: build DeseqStats with `lfc_null=1.0, alt_hypothesis="greaterAbs"`, which recomputes the Wald test against that null and yields valid p-values and padj for |LFC| > 1.
recommendations.install:
In your DE script, for the effect-size question use:
stat_res = DeseqStats(dds, contrast=["condition", "treated", "control"], lfc_null=1.0, alt_hypothesis="greaterAbs")

And add to C:\Users\Manec\bio-stack\tests\test_deseq_guardrails.py (~10 lines):
p_before = stat_res.results_df[["pvalue", "padj"]].copy()
stat_res.lfc_shrink(coeff="condition[T.treated]")
assert stat_res.results_df[["pvalue", "padj"]].equals(p_before)  # shrinkage must not touch inference
recommendations.why: Reporting a shrunk LFC as if it carried its own significance is a real, checkable error that a banca can catch by reading two columns. The supported alternative exists in the same installed version and produces defensible padj for a stated biological effect size, which is strictly better than an arbitrary post-hoc cutoff.
recommendations.caveat: `lfc_null=1.0` changes what is being tested, so results are not comparable to a standard lfc_null=0 run — report which one produced each figure. Also never run statsmodels `multipletests` on PyDESeq2 output: padj is already adjusted and you would be double-correcting.

recommendations.title: State that scanpy's FDR is per-group, not family-wide — and never report a padj from method='logreg'
recommendations.what: In the installed scanpy 1.11.5 (.venv\Lib\site-packages\scanpy\tools\_rank_genes_groups.py, block at L462-473), the BH correction sits INSIDE the per-group loop: `multipletests(pvals, alpha=0.05, method="fdr_bh")` is called once per group, so the family is one group's gene set — there is no correction across the joint groups x genes family. Genes with undefined statistics (zero variance in both groups) get scores set to 0 and p = 1 upstream before correction, so no NaN reaches the reported column. With `method='logreg'` there are no p-values at all: `pvals` is None, so neither `pvals` nor `pvals_adj` is created — yet `corr_method='benjamini-hochberg'` is still recorded in `adata.uns[key]['params']`, meaning /metodos will draft a Methods sentence claiming an FDR that was never applied.

Paste into your Methods draft verbatim and adapt:

Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (statsmodels v0.15.0, method='fdr_bh', alpha=0.05) was applied independently within each comparison group's gene set, not across the joint groups x genes family. Genes with undefined test statistics (zero variance in both groups) were assigned p = 1 by scanpy before correction."

Reproduce the evidence in PowerShell:

The logreg trap is worse: it silently produces a Methods sentence that is factually false, and this project's provenance hook + /metodos pipeline will propagate it automatically unless you strip it by hand.

uv run pytest --randomly-seed=last
Isolate with:
uv run pytest -p no:randomly
recommendations.why: A seed in the code is a claim; a test that runs the stochastic step twice and compares output is evidence. This is the cheapest falsifiable artifact you can put in the repo to back the reproducibility sentence in Methods.
recommendations.caveat: pytest-randomly reseeds only NumPy's LEGACY RandomState — a `np.random.default_rng()` Generator is NOT reset by the plugin, so construct every Generator explicitly inside the test from a literal seed rather than relying on it. Since 4.0.0 the seed is derived per-test from the test ID (CRC32), so `--randomly-seed=last` replays the session base seed, not a single per-test value you can lift into a script. `--randomly-seed=last` also depends on pytest's cacheprovider, so it silently stops replaying under `-p no:cacheprovider`.

recommendations.title: Pin leiden flavor/n_iterations/directed and record UMAP's single-thread cost in Methods
recommendations.what: In the installed scanpy 1.11.5, `tl.leiden` still defaults to `flavor="leidenalg"` with `n_iterations=-1` (.venv\Lib\site-packages\scanpy\tools\_leiden.py L41,46) and carries an in-source FutureWarning that the default backend will become igraph and that you should pass `flavor="igraph", n_iterations=2` (and `directed=False`). Partitions differ between flavors, so the flavor must be pinned alongside the seed or the seed guarantees nothing across a scanpy upgrade. Separately, `tl.umap` defaults `random_state=0` (_umap.py L52), and UMAP's own docs state that setting a random_state "effectively turn[s] off any of the multi-threading that does not support explicit reproducibility", with a measured wall-clock cost — that trade is a Methods fact, not an implementation detail.
recommendations.install:
In your clustering script call exactly:

sc.tl.umap(adata, random_state=0)

And add to Methods: "Leiden clustering used the igraph backend with n_iterations=2, directed=False and random_state=0 (scanpy v1.11.5); UMAP was run with random_state=0, which disables non-reproducible multi-threading in umap-learn."
recommendations.why: "random_state=0" alone is not a reproducibility claim when the algorithm behind it can change backend on upgrade. Naming flavor, iteration count and directedness makes the clustering step re-runnable by someone who only has your Methods paragraph.
recommendations.caveat: Switching from leidenalg to igraph changes your cluster labels, so do it before you start interpreting clusters, not after — and never mid-analysis.
