recommendations.title: Report a family-wide FDR over groups x genes as a sensitivity analysis, not as a replacement
recommendations.what: If a reviewer asks for control across the joint family, recompute it yourself rather than re-running scanpy: `df = sc.get.rank_genes_groups_df(adata, group=None)` gives the tidy frame, then `rej, padj_global, _, _ = multipletests(df['pvals'].to_numpy(), alpha=0.05, method='fdr_bh')`. Report both numbers. Do NOT flatten `adata.uns[key]['pvals']` directly — its rows are ordered by rank within each group, so gene identity differs across columns.
recommendations.install:
Add to your DE script (~6 lines):
import scanpy as sc
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests
df = sc.get.rank_genes_groups_df(adata, group=None)
rej, padj_global, _, _ = multipletests(df["pvals"].to_numpy(), alpha=0.05, method="fdr_bh")
df["pvals_adj_global"] = padj_global
recommendations.why: It costs six lines and pre-empts the most likely statistical objection to a multi-cluster DE table, while keeping the default per-group numbers as the primary result so the figures do not change.
recommendations.caveat: Only valid as a joint family when rank_genes_groups ran with n_genes=None (the installed 1.11.5 default) and groups='all' — with n_genes=N the flattened vector is a truncated, selection-biased subset and BH's denominator is wrong. Also, under the default reference='rest' each group is tested against all remaining cells, so the per-group tests share cells and are positively dependent; BH's guarantee holds under independence/PRDS, so present the global number as a sensitivity analysis, or use method='fdr_by' (Benjamini-Yekutieli, valid under arbitrary dependence, present in statsmodels 0.15.0) if a dependence-robust bound is demanded.

recommendations.title: If you want an adaptive FDR, use statsmodels fdr_tsbh with a declared alpha — do not adopt multipy
recommendations.what: statsmodels 0.15.0 is already installed and exposes `method='fdr_tsbh'` (two-stage Benjamini-Krieger-Yekutieli) in the same `multipletests` call. Call it adaptive two-stage BH, not "Storey q-value" — they are different procedures. The main Python Storey q-value package, github.com/puolival/multipy, is effectively dead: last commit 2020-10-27, last PyPI release 0.16 on 2019-04-18 — nearly six years without a commit as of 2026-09-14. Its PyPI name also collides with PyTorch's unrelated torch::deploy project, so if you cite it at all, cite the GitHub repo, never the bare package name.
recommendations.install:
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests
rej, padj, _, _ = multipletests(pvals, alpha=0.05, method="fdr_tsbh")  # alpha is load-bearing, report it
recommendations.why: An adaptive procedure gains power when the true null proportion is well below 1, and you get it with zero new dependencies and no abandoned package in your Methods section.
recommendations.caveat: Unlike fdr_bh, the fdr_tsbh adjusted p-values DEPEND on alpha (verified: on 200 p-values, padj[0] = 0.0728 at alpha=0.05 but 0.0648 at alpha=0.10). You must pass the alpha you will actually threshold at and state it — you cannot present tsbh adjusted p-values as an alpha-free quantity in a figure legend.

#: Versao do formato de cada linha. O arquivo ja mudou de forma uma vez sem
#: aviso (linhas antigas nao tem `ok` nem `commit`), e um leitor que assuma o
#: formato novo quebra ou, pior, mente sobre as linhas velhas.
SCHEMA = 3


def _commit() -> str | None:
    """
    SHA do HEAD, lido direto do diretorio .git.

    Poderia ser `git rev-parse HEAD`, mas isso e um subprocesso por chamada de
    ferramenta — em 900 operacoes, minutos de overhead. Ler o arquivo custa
    microssegundos e da a mesma resposta.

    Isto e o que amarra resultado a codigo. Sem o SHA, o log responde "o que eu
    rodei" mas nao "com qual versao do script" — e a segunda pergunta e a que
    torna o resultado reproduzivel.
    """
    raiz = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2] / ".git"
    try:
        head = (raiz / "HEAD").read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip()
    except OSError:
        return None
    if not head.startswith("ref:"):
        return head[:40] or None  # HEAD destacado ja e o proprio SHA

    ref = head[4:].strip()
    try:
        return (raiz / ref).read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip()[:40]
    except OSError:
        pass
    # Ref empacotada: depois de `git gc` o arquivo solto deixa de existir.
    try:
        for linha in (raiz / "packed-refs").read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
            if linha.endswith(f" {ref}"):
                return linha.split(" ", 1)[0][:40]
    except OSError:
        pass
    return None


COMMIT = _commit()

# /// script

# dependencies = ["scanpy==1.11.5", "numpy==2.4.6", "igraph>=0.11", "leidenalg>=0.10"]
# ///
"""
Verifica que semente fixada realmente produz o mesmo resultado nesta instalacao.

Isto nao e paranoia. UMAP e Leiden sao estocasticos, e "fixei a semente" e uma
afirmacao que quase ninguem testa — a pessoa roda uma vez, ve um numero, e
assume. Quando o resultado muda entre execucoes, muda silenciosamente: nenhum
erro, so uma figura diferente e uma contagem de cluster diferente.

Roda sobre matriz sintetica de proposito. Determinismo e propriedade do codigo,
nao do dado; usar dado real tornaria o teste lento e dependente de download.

    uv run --script tests/test_determinism.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import sys
import warnings

import numpy as np
import scanpy as sc

SEMENTE = 0
N_CELULAS, N_GENES = 300, 200

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
sc.settings.verbosity = 0


def matriz():
    """
    Contagens sinteticas com estrutura de grupo, para que o Leiden tenha o que
    particionar. Sem estrutura, todas as celulas caem num cluster so e o teste
    passaria sem exercitar nada.

    Gerador proprio e explicito: `pytest-randomly` reseeda apenas o RandomState
    legado do numpy, nunca um Generator. Confiar nele aqui seria testar o
    plugin, nao o pipeline.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(12345)
    base = rng.negative_binomial(5, 0.3, size=(N_CELULAS, N_GENES)).astype("float32")
    base[: N_CELULAS // 2, : N_GENES // 4] *= 4  # um subgrupo com perfil distinto
    ad = sc.AnnData(base)
    ad.var_names = [f"gene{i}" for i in range(N_GENES)]
    ad.obs_names = [f"cel{i}" for i in range(N_CELULAS)]
    return ad


def pipeline():
    """Normaliza, PCA, vizinhos, UMAP e Leiden — tudo com semente declarada."""
    ad = matriz()
    sc.pp.normalize_total(ad, target_sum=1e4)
    sc.pp.log1p(ad)
    sc.pp.pca(ad, n_comps=20, random_state=SEMENTE)
    sc.pp.neighbors(ad, n_neighbors=15, random_state=SEMENTE)

WSL_TOOLS = {
    "nextflow": "pipelines nf-core",
    "nf-core": "lint e scaffold de pipeline",
    "samtools": "manipulacao de BAM",
    "bcftools": "manipulacao de VCF",
    "bedtools": "operacoes de intervalo",
    "seqkit": "manipulacao de FASTA/FASTQ",
}


def _wsl_presentes() -> set[str] | None:
    """
    Quais ferramentas respondem dentro da distro. `None` = WSL indisponivel.

    Uma unica chamada resolve todas: abrir o WSL custa ~1s, e fazer isso seis
    vezes tornaria o hook de inicio de sessao perceptivelmente lento.
    """
    if not shutil.which("wsl"):
        return None
    alvos = " ".join(WSL_TOOLS)
    try:
        proc = subprocess.run(
            ["wsl", "-d", WSL_DISTRO, "--", "bash", "-lc",

        return None
    if proc.returncode != 0:
        return None
    return {ln.strip() for ln in proc.stdout.replace("\x00", "").splitlines() if ln.strip()}

WSL2 com Ubuntu-24.04: a camada Linux que faltava

Instalado na distro: nextflow 26.04.6, nf-core 4.1.0, samtools 1.19.2,
bcftools 1.19, bedtools 2.31.1, seqkit 2.13.0, tabix, Java 21. Verificado ponta

abortava por falta do Nextflow, nao por bug proprio.

seguiria dizendo "ausente" com tudo instalado e funcionando.

wsl.exe engole sequencias de variavel na traducao da linha de comando. Um laco
`for t in ...; do echo ...; done` executa o numero certo de vezes e imprime
vazio em todas, sem erro e sem stderr. A sonda foi reescrita sem cifrao nenhum —
`command -v` aceita varios nomes de uma vez.

O guard de dados barrou o instalador do Nextflow por ser script encanado direto
para o shell, corretamente. O script foi baixado, conferido (Apache 2.0, Seqera
Labs, sha256 registrado) e so entao executado.

Pendente e fora do meu alcance: a integracao WSL do Docker Desktop esta
desligada para Ubuntu-24.04, entao nao ha docker dentro da distro e os pipelines
nf-core rodam so com -profile conda ou singularity.

input.question: Comparative genomics project plan: Psittaciformes (parrots) versus Crocodylia/Neosuchia — what genome data (accessions, assembly quality), methods, tools and MCP servers are needed to characterise the genomic differences and similarities across the ~240-255 Myr archosaur divergence, and to reconstruct ancestral sequence states and lineage-specific molecular changes, on a 20-core / 15 GB RAM / 8 GB VRAM workstation with no cluster.
input.summary: The question bundles five separable research problems: what data actually exists with accessions, how to orthologise and align genomes at deep divergence under hard hardware limits, how to test for selection without the known false-positive traps, what ancestral reconstruction and molecular dating can honestly claim, and which parrot-vs-crocodilian biological questions already have published precedent. Queries are therefore split by evidence type — assembly registries, resource/benchmark reports, methodological critiques, ASR/dating primary literature, and clade-specific comparative genomics — rather than by keyword variation, so each returns a different corpus.

angles.label: data availability / primary accessions
angles.query: Vertebrate Genomes Project B10K chromosome-level genome assembly Strigops habroptila Melopsittacus undulatus Amazona Ara macao and Alligator mississippiensis Crocodylus porosus Gavialis gangeticus NCBI RefSeq annotation accession contig N50
angles.rationale: Surfaces GenomeArk/VGP/B10K release pages, NCBI assembly reports and the genome announcement papers carrying accessions, assembly level, N50 and whether a RefSeq GFF annotation exists — the (a) deliverable — plus turtle/lepidosaur outgroup assemblies needed to polarise changes.

angles.label: alignment & orthology feasibility / resource benchmarks
angles.query: Progressive Cactus whole-genome alignment memory RAM requirements CPU hours vertebrate genomes benchmark versus LASTZ chain net minimap2 asm20 OrthoFinder BUSCO sauropsida runtime single workstation no cluster
angles.rationale: Targets the hardware-reality question: documented RAM and wall-clock for Cactus, LASTZ/chains-nets and OrthoFinder on 1.2-2.5 Gb sauropsid genomes, to decide what fits 15 GB RAM / 20 cores versus what needs a cluster; should also surface nf-core/pairgenomealign and Bioconda/Docker packaging.

angles.label: contrarian / methodological critique of selection tests
angles.query: branch-site test false positives critique Venkat Hahn alignment error synonymous saturation deep divergence GC-biased gene conversion PAML codeml HyPhy aBSREL BUSTED RELAX best practice codon alignment PRANK HmmCleaner trimAl
angles.rationale: The (c) deliverable — the statistical pitfalls. Deliberately skeptical framing pulls the critique and rebuttal literature (Venkat et al. 2018 and responses, Fletcher & Yang alignment-error work, gBGC confounding) rather than tool manuals, plus current guidance on upstream codon alignment and trimming.

angles.label: ASR epistemic limits and molecular dating of the split
angles.query: ancestral sequence reconstruction accuracy bias consensus thermostability artifact limits inferring order of substitutions along a branch; bird crocodilian Archosauria crown divergence time fossil calibrated estimate confidence interval TimeTree
angles.rationale: Covers (d), what '250 Myr of mutations' can and cannot answer, by pairing ASR accuracy/bias assessments (Thornton, Gaucher thermostability-bias debate, marginal vs joint reconstruction caveats in IQ-TREE/FastML/GRASP) with primary fossil-calibrated archosaur divergence dates to check whether ~250 Myr is defensible.

angles.label: clade-specific precedent / defensible research questions
angles.query: parrot genome evolution comparative analysis vocal learning genes longevity telomere beta-keratin gene family olfactory receptor repertoire contraction crocodilian slow molecular evolutionary rate positive selection Psittaciformes published studies
angles.rationale: The scope and (e) deliverable: identifies which candidate gene sets already have parrot and crocodilian comparative-genomics precedent to anchor an undergraduate-scale question, and surfaces the crocodilian slow-substitution-rate literature that directly conditions any rate or selection comparison.

input.prompt: Report the assembly name, accession (GCA and GCF), assembly level, contig N50, scaffold N50, genome size, number of chromosomes, submitter/project (VGP?), and whether a RefSeq annotation (GFF) exists with its annotation release date and gene count.
What divergence time (in millions of years ago) does this paper state for the split between birds and crocodilians / the crown Archosauria split? Quote the exact figure and any confidence interval.

Summarize the key findings about accuracy and systematic bias of ancestral protein reconstruction methods — especially any statement about accumulation of small per-site errors biasing whole-sequence properties like thermostability, and differences between parsimony, ML and Bayesian methods.

results.title: Harvard FAS Informatics — Whole-genome alignment with Progressive Cactus (tutorial + Snakemake pipeline)
results.snippet: The most directly actionable hardware verdict found: the tutorial states requirements depend on genome size and divergence but are 'roughly 64 cores / 512G RAM ... for distant mammals', and the group ships a Snakemake wrapper explicitly designed to run Cactus ON A CLUSTER (SLURM), splitting the job into per-node blast/align steps. Bird-vs-crocodilian (~1.2-2.5 Gb, ~250 Myr) is at least as diverged as 'distant mammals', so this is the clearest published statement that Progressive Cactus does NOT fit 15 GB RAM / 20 cores and must be flagged as cluster-only for this project. Companion tutorials (add-genome, add-outgroup, replace-genome to an existing HAL) matter for the outgroup-polarisation step.

results.title: Armstrong et al. — Progressive Cactus is a multiple-genome aligner for the thousand-genome era (Nature 2020)
results.snippet: Primary source for Cactus resource benchmarks: the vertebrate alignment benchmark used a 64-CPU / 1 TB RAM machine plus a ~1000-CPU shared cluster; the largest single target consumed ~100 GB RAM, peak ~250 GB, at roughly a day wall-clock and just under 100 CPU-days per genome aligned. Runtime scales linearly in number of genomes (progressive decomposition), but per-node memory does not shrink — so even a 2-genome bird/croc job inherits the 100 GB-class peak. Also the source for the 600+ amniote alignment (Zoonomia/B10K-adjacent HALs) the project could DOWNLOAD instead of computing, which is the real recommendation for this hardware.

results.title: ComparativeGenomicsToolkit/cactus — progressive.md (official run + hardware/packaging docs)
results.snippet: Official current docs for the maintained Cactus (the older glennhickey/progressiveCactus repo is dead and must not be recommended). Covers the release binaries, Docker image and --binariesMode local|docker toggle, Toil batch-system backends (single_machine vs slurm), and the hal2maf/HAL toolchain needed to extract per-gene alignments. Also the packaging answer: a `cactus` Bioconda recipe exists (bioconda.github.io/recipes/cactus) but Minigraph-Cactus is x86-only and unsupported on Mac/ARM; the Docker route is what works under WSL2 Docker Desktop. Note the counterpoint in the pangenome docs that small dm6 (Drosophila, 140 Mb) graphs were built on 32 cores / 16 GB RAM — i.e. 15 GB is a fly-scale budget, not a sauropsid-scale one.

results.title: Emms et al. — OrthoFinder v3: improved phylogenetic orthology inference with enhanced accuracy and scalability (Nature Methods 2026)
results.snippet: The orthology half of the feasibility question, and the good news for this hardware: 80 VERTEBRATE proteomes (1.7 M sequences) were analysed on a 2015 desktop with 4 cores and 8 GB RAM in 20 hours. v3's linear-addition mode cuts RAM ~3.4x versus v2 DendroBlast at 256 species and was the only method to finish 1,024 species inside 7 days. Implication for the plan: a ~10-20 proteome Psittaciformes + Crocodylia + Testudines/Lepidosauria/Mammalia outgroup set is comfortably a laptop-scale OrthoFinder job on 20 cores / 15 GB RAM — so build the project on protein-level orthology (OrthoFinder + BUSCO sauropsida/aves lineage sets) rather than on whole-genome alignment. Includes the 8-64 species core-set guideline for the add-species workflow.

results.title: nf-core/pairgenomealign — pairwise genome alignment with LAST (docs + usage)
results.snippet: The realistic Nextflow-native whole-genome-alignment option on this box: lastdb indexing, lastal pairwise alignment with trainable scoring (LAST's strength is exactly distant/diverged pairs, unlike minimap2), last-dotplot plots, and maf-convert export to SAM/BAM/CRAM/PAF — all Bioconda/Docker containerised and already runnable given the verified `nextflow -profile docker` setup under WSL2. Usage docs carry the two resource landmines to guard against on 15 GB RAM: --m2m (many-to-many alignment) 'can exhaust computing resources in the case of very large genomes', and the tandem-repeat masking unit length that had to be capped at 400 to avoid OOM on centromeric repeats. Also the entry point for tuning lastdb seeding to sauropsid-scale genomes.

results.title: Song et al. — AnchorWave: sensitive alignment of genomes with high sequence diversity, extensive structural polymorphism (PNAS 2022)
results.snippet: Underpins the negative result the plan needs to state explicitly: minimap2's whole-genome presets terminate extension at ~5% (asm5), ~10% (asm10) and ~20% (asm20) divergence, its documented full-genome use case is closely related species below ~15% divergence, and sensitivity collapses at higher divergence because k-mer matches are filtered during chaining. Bird-vs-crocodilian neutral divergence far exceeds that, so `minimap2 -x asm20` is the wrong tool at 250 Myr and should be cut from the plan except for within-Psittaciformes or within-Crocodylia pairs. AnchorWave's anchor-then-align strategy (and, separately, LASTZ/chain/net) is the sensitivity-preserving alternative, though AnchorWave's anchoring assumes usable gene annotations on both sides.

results.title: Wirthlin et al. 2018, Current Biology — Parrot Genomes and the Evolution of Heightened Longevity and Cognition
results.snippet: The single strongest precedent paper for the parrot half of the project. High-coverage annotated Amazona aestiva genome compared against 30 other birds including 4 other parrots, using exactly the toolchain the user has (ortholog sets + branch/branch-site selection tests + gene-family expansion). Delivers three ready-made, citable candidate gene sets for an undergrad-scale question: (1) longevity/telomere-maintenance genes (telomerase activity, DNA damage repair, cell-cycle/cancer control, anti-oxidative genes), (2) parrot-specific novel genes and parrot-specific changes in coding AND regulatory (accelerated conserved non-exonic element) sequence, (3) vocal-learning circuitry — notably PLXNC1, uniquely duplicated in parrots and differentially expressed in the vocal-learning motor cortex of humans, parrots and hummingbirds. A defensible TCC scope is to replicate one of these gene sets with a crocodilian outgroup added, rather than invent a new scan.

results.title: Green et al. 2014, Science — Three crocodilian genomes reveal ancestral patterns of evolution among archosaurs
results.snippet: The crocodilian half, and the paper that conditions every rate or selection comparison the project will run. Draft genomes of Alligator mississippiensis, Crocodylus porosus and Gavialis gangeticus; documents an exceptionally slow rate of genome evolution in crocodilians at every level — nucleotide substitution, indels, transposable element content and movement, gene family turnover, chromosomal synteny — roughly an order of magnitude slower than mammals, attributed to long generation time. Two direct consequences for the user's plan: (a) any branch-length or dN/dS comparison between a parrot branch and a crocodilian branch is confounded by lineage-specific rate, so RELAX / free-ratio models and rate-normalisation are mandatory rather than optional; (b) the paper explicitly reconstructs a partial ancestral archosaur genome from crocodilian + bird data, which is the published precedent (and the realistic ceiling) for the user's 'reconstruct what changed over ~250 Myr' ambition — probable ancestral states at the archosaur node, not a mutation timeline.

results.title: Vandewege et al. 2016, Genome Biology and Evolution — Contrasting Patterns of Evolutionary Diversification in the Olfactory Repertoires of Reptile and Bird Genomes
results.snippet: Gives the olfactory-receptor angle real numbers and a published baseline to reproduce, and it already spans both target clades. Sauropsid OR repertoires vary over an order of magnitude (108 intact genes in Anolis to 1,180 in Chinese softshell turtle; pseudogenes from 33 in Anolis to 538 in Alligator mississippiensis), with OR5/8/9 expanded in predatory birds and alligator. This is the most tractable candidate family for 15 GB RAM: OR repertoire annotation is an HMM/BLAST-style scan of assemblies plus intact-vs-pseudogene calling, not a whole-genome alignment, so it fits the hardware. Caveat to flag in the plan: repertoire counts are strongly sensitive to assembly contiguity and annotation pipeline, so parrot-vs-crocodilian count differences must be controlled for assembly quality (VGP chromosome-level vs 2014-era crocodilian scaffolds) before any biological claim.

results.title: Greenwold & Sawyer 2010, BMC Evolutionary Biology — Genomic organization and molecular phylogenies of the beta-keratin multigene family (chicken, zebra finch): implications for feather evolution
results.snippet: The beta-keratin precedent, and the cleanest archosaur-scale gene-family story available to an undergrad. Establishes the subfamily structure (scale, claw, feather-like, feather) clustered in 5'-3' order on microchromosome 25, with avian scale beta-keratins sister to crocodilian beta-keratins and basal to claw, which is basal to feather/feather-like. The gene-count contrast is the hook: >100 beta-keratin genes in chicken and zebra finch versus 20 in American alligator and 21 in saltwater crocodile — a shared-ancestral versus bird-derived expansion that is directly testable with CAFE5 gene-family birth-death modelling plus a phylogeny of the cluster, and does not need Progressive Cactus. No parrot-specific beta-keratin catalogue appears to be published, which makes 'annotate the beta-keratin cluster in Psittaciformes and place it against crocodilian and galliform references' a genuinely novel but modest, well-anchored TCC question. See also the companion Greenwold et al. 2014 BMC Evol Biol paper on dynamic alpha/beta keratin evolution across a wider archosaur sampling.

results.title: Pfenning et al. 2014, Science — Convergent transcriptional specializations in the brains of humans and song-learning birds
results.snippet: The companion to the B10K/avian phylogenomics package (Jarvis et al. and Zhang et al. 2014, Science) and the source of the vocal-learning gene lists that Wirthlin 2018 builds on. Identifies convergent gene expression specializations in song and speech nuclei shared between vocal-learning birds (parrots among them) and human laryngeal motor cortex/striatum, with most associated genes in motor control and brain connectivity. Relevance to this project is as a candidate-gene supplier and a cautionary framing: the signal is expression-level convergence, not sequence convergence, and parrots and crocodilians have no shared vocal-learning phenotype — so a parrot-vs-crocodilian test of these genes is a test of bird-lineage derivation against an archosaur baseline, not a convergence test. Useful for defining the gene panel; not usable on its own to justify a selection claim.

results.title: Dussex et al. 2021, Cell Genomics — Population genomics of the critically endangered kakapo
results.snippet: Precedent for the highest-quality parrot assembly in the stack and a worked example of ancestral-allele polarisation using a sister parrot. Strigops habroptila was among the first chromosome-level VGP reference genomes (released 2018, Jarvis/Rockefeller); the study adds 35 modern island and 14 extinct mainland genomes and uses the kea (Nestor notabilis) alignment explicitly for ancestral allele inference in mutational load analysis. Two takeaways for the plan: (a) Strigops habroptila and Nestor notabilis are the assembly-quality anchors on the parrot side — pairing a VGP chromosome-level parrot with the 2014-era scaffold-level crocodilians is the main technical asymmetry to declare; (b) the Strigops lineage diverged from other parrots ~82 Mya, which gives the project a useful within-Psittaciformes depth axis and a concrete demonstration of using a close relative to polarise changes — the same logic the user needs applied at the archosaur node with Testudines and Lepidosauria outgroups.

results.title: Alligator mississippiensis genome assembly rAllMis1 (GCF_030867095.1) — NCBI Datasets
results.snippet: The current best crocodilian reference and the single most important accession for deliverable (a). rAllMis1 is a modern VGP-style long-read/Hi-C assembly of the American alligator that supersedes the 2012 ASM28112v4 draft (GCA_000281125.4 / GCF_000281125.x, allMis0.2), which was scaffold-level with a short contig N50 and is what most published bird-vs-croc comparisons still use. Because it is a GCF (RefSeq) accession it carries an NCBI Eukaryotic Genome Annotation Pipeline GFF3 plus protein and CDS FASTA, so it can feed OrthoFinder/BUSCO/codeml directly without running genome annotation locally — critical given no R/Bioconductor and 15 GB RAM. Pull with `datasets download genome accession GCF_030867095.1 --include genome,gff3,protein,cds,rna`; ~2.2 Gb genome, expect roughly 1 GB compressed. Verify assembly level, contig/scaffold N50 and annotation release date on this page before committing — the page is JS-rendered, so use `datasets summary genome accession GCF_030867095.1` from the WSL CLI rather than scraping it.

results.title: Melopsittacus undulatus genome assembly bMelUnd1.mat.Z (GCF_012275295.1) — NCBI Datasets
results.snippet: The reference-quality Psittaciformes anchor. VGP/G10K trio assembly submitted April 2020: chromosome level, 1,148 contigs into 864 scaffolds, 32 chromosomes built, contig N50 16,636,420 bp and scaffold N50 104,092,594 bp — two orders of magnitude better contiguity than the 2012 Melopsittacus_undulatus_6.3 draft (GCF_000238935.1, melUnd1) that is still widely cited and should NOT be used for synteny. Has RefSeq annotation (NCBI annotation release 104) and an Ensembl gene set, so the budgerigar gives you both a RefSeq GFF and an Ensembl/Compara entry point — useful because Ensembl provides precomputed orthologs that can sanity-check your own OrthoFinder run. Chromosome-level status is what makes MCScanX/GENESPACE synteny and LASTZ chain/net against the alligator tractable; scaffold-level parrots are not.

results.title: Strigops habroptila (kākāpō) RefSeq Annotation Report — assembly bStrHab1.2.pri (GCF_004027225.2)
results.snippet: Confirms a full NCBI RefSeq gene set exists for the kākāpō, the second reference-grade parrot and one of the flagship first VGP assemblies (GenBank GCA_004027225.2 primary, GCA_004011185.1 alternate haplotype; BioProject PRJNA489134). Reported genome 1.06 Gb with contig N50 5.6 Mb, largest contig 29.3 Mb. The annotation report page is the thing to read for the (a) deliverable because it states the annotation release, the RNA-seq evidence used and the counts of protein-coding genes — i.e. whether the GFF is good enough to mine 1:1 orthologs for codeml, or whether missing/fragmented models will inflate false positives in branch-site tests. Kākāpō + budgerigar gives two deeply divergent parrot lineages (Strigopoidea vs Psittaculidae, crown Psittaciformes), which is the minimum sampling needed to place a change on the parrot stem rather than on a single terminal branch.

results.title: Gavialis gangeticus genome assembly GavGan_comp1 (GCF_001723915.1) — NCBI Datasets
results.snippet: The gharial accession, and the third crocodilian needed to polarise changes inside Crocodylia (Alligatoridae / Crocodylidae / Gavialidae). Named *_comp1 because it is a Ragout comparative-scaffolding product built by projecting the short-read draft onto the chromosome-scale alligator — so its 'chromosome-scale' apparent contiguity is largely inherited, not independently observed. That matters concretely: do not use GavGan_comp1 for synteny or breakpoint claims, only for gene-level orthology and codon alignments, and say so in Methods. It does carry a RefSeq GFF, so it is usable as a third ingroup tip for PAML/HyPhy branch models where three crocodilians let you fit a crocodilian stem branch.

results.title: A High-Quality Reference Genome Assembly of the Saltwater Crocodile, Crocodylus porosus, Reveals Patterns of Selection in Crocodylidae (Genome Biol. Evol. 2020)
results.snippet: The genome announcement carrying the C. porosus accessions and, crucially, the assembly caveats: it names Cpor_2.0 (GCA_000768395.1, AllPaths-LG from Illumina short-insert/mate-pair) and CroPor_comp1 (GCF_001723895.1, Ragout comparative scaffolding onto the alligator) as the two pre-existing annotated drafts, then presents the improved long-read assembly. Directly relevant as published precedent for the project's selection-analysis angle — it is a worked bird-and-crocodilian-context selection scan on exactly these genomes, so it supplies both the ortholog-set construction recipe and a result the student can attempt to reproduce. Also the reference for the older International Crocodilian Genomes Working Group trio (alligator, saltwater croc, gharial) whose 2012 Genome Biology paper is the origin of the low-contiguity drafts still lurking in NCBI.

results.title: Chrysemys picta bellii genome assembly (GCF_011386835.1) — NCBI Datasets
results.snippet: The outgroup accession that makes the whole polarisation argument work. Turtles are the sister group to Archosauria, so without a Testudines tip you cannot tell an apomorphic parrot change from a retained archosaur ancestral state — every 'lineage-specific mutation over 250 Myr' claim depends on this. Painted turtle has a RefSeq GFF and a newer chromosome-level assembly (SLU_Cpb5.0, 25 pseudochromosomes) described in a 2025 bioRxiv preprint, so check for a superseding GCF before downloading. A defensible minimum sampling is 2 parrots + 1 non-parrot bird (chicken GCF_016699485.1 as the best-annotated avian) + 2–3 crocodilians + this turtle + a lepidosaur (Anolis carolinensis, AnoCar2.0 — first non-avian reptile genome, but old and fragmented, so flag its annotation quality) + one mammal to root. That is ~8–9 proteomes, which is comfortably within 15 GB RAM for OrthoFinder.

results.title: Venkat, Hahn & Thornton (2018) — Multinucleotide mutations cause false inferences of lineage-specific positive selection (Nat Ecol Evol; free PMC full text)
results.snippet: The central critique for deliverable (c). The branch-site test (PAML codeml Model A / Test 2) assumes nucleotide substitutions occur singly and independently; multinucleotide mutations (MNMs, ~0.4–2% of mutations) are overwhelmingly nonsynonymous and violate that assumption. Codons with multiple differences account for virtually all support for lineage-specific positive selection in real data, and simulations with realistic MNM rates produce false positives at roughly the same rate the BST reports 'selection' empirically. Direct consequence for the parrot-vs-crocodilian plan: any codeml branch-site hit must be re-checked after masking or down-weighting multi-difference codons on the focal branch (or fit an MNM-aware codon model, e.g. the generalized parametric codon models of Jones et al. 2018 BMC Ecol Evol), otherwise the 'lineage-specific adaptation in Psittaciformes' result is not defensible in a TCC. Note there is no formal published Dunn/Zou/Zhang-style rebuttal — the finding stands and should be treated as a required control, not a controversy.

results.title: Bolívar et al. (2019) — GC-biased gene conversion conceals the prediction of the nearly neutral theory in avian genomes (Genome Biology, open access)
results.snippet: Bird-specific confounder, directly on the Psittaciformes side of the comparison. gBGC preferentially fixes S (G/C) over W (A/T) alleles near recombination-initiated double-strand breaks, acts more strongly on synonymous than nonsynonymous sites, and therefore deflates dS and inflates dN/dS — mimicking positive selection and breaking the expected correlation between dN/dS and life-history traits in birds. Avian genomes have exceptionally heterogeneous recombination landscapes and strong gBGC, so a naive parrot-branch dN/dS scan will preferentially flag high-recombination, GC-rich, often subtelomeric genes. Practical guard: annotate every candidate with GC3 / GC* and W→S substitution polarity, and either exclude gBGC-suspect genes or run a gBGC-aware model (companion work: Bolívar et al. 2018 MBE on flycatchers, https://academic.oup.com/mbe/advance-article/doi/10.1093/molbev/msy149/5063898; reptile/vertebrate baseline: Figuet et al. 2015 GBE, https://academic.oup.com/gbe/article/7/1/240/602048).

results.title: Jordan & Goldman (2012) — Effects of alignment error and alignment filtering on the sitewise detection of positive selection (Mol Biol Evol 29:1125)
results.snippet: Quantifies how much the upstream alignment choice changes the answer — the single biggest lever in this project, since ~250 Myr divergence maximises indel and alignment ambiguity. Building on Fletcher & Yang (2010), false-positive rates for the branch-site test reach up to 0.99 with ClustalW alignments under some indel scenarios. PRANK codon-aware alignments consistently perform best but still hit ~0.13 FPR (vs. nominal 0.05). Of the filters, GUIDANCE performs best and Gblocks worst — but no filter substantially improves already-good PRANK alignments, so filtering is not a rescue for a bad aligner. Concrete recommendation for the stack: align codons with PRANK (+F) or MACSE rather than back-translated MAFFT, score with GUIDANCE2, and report selection results both filtered and unfiltered as a sensitivity analysis.

results.title: Álvarez-Carretero, Kapli & Yang (2023) — Beginner's Guide on the Use of PAML to Detect Positive Selection (Mol Biol Evol 40:msad041)
results.snippet: Current canonical best-practice protocol from Yang's own group, and the document that tells you which pitfalls PAML's authors themselves consider real. Covers: which codeml models to use and which are obsolete, the correct LRT degrees of freedom and the conservative 50:50 chi-square mixture for branch-site Test 2, the need for multiple starting values of omega/kappa to avoid local optima, the requirement that the focal branch be specified a priori (not chosen after seeing the data — otherwise the test is invalid), and that the BEB posterior identifies sites only conditional on the LRT being significant. Also the standard convention that genome-wide scans require FDR/Benjamini–Hochberg correction across genes. This is the source to cite in the Methods section for every codeml parameter choice.

results.title: Tan et al. (2015) — Current methods for automated filtering of multiple sequence alignments frequently worsen single-gene phylogenetic inference (Syst Biol 64:778)
results.snippet: The counterweight to 'just run trimAl and move on'. Gblocks and BMGE at default settings have excessively low tolerance for gap-containing columns and remove informative residues; Gblocks defaults reduced tree accuracy in half the tested scenarios, and even with tuned parameters most filters did not beat unfiltered alignments for amino-acid data. Matters here because the whole downstream chain (gene trees → species tree → branch labelling → codeml/HyPhy → ancestral reconstruction) inherits alignment-trimming decisions, and over-trimming at deep divergence throws away exactly the variable sites that carry the lineage signal. Suggests preferring signal-aware trimmers (ClipKIT, https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.3001007; PhyIN, https://peerj.com/articles/18504/) over Gblocks, and documenting the trimming setting as a reported sensitivity parameter rather than a silent default.

results.title: Minus the Error: Testing for Positive Selection in the Presence of Residual Alignment Errors (eLife reviewed preprint, 106921)
results.snippet: Recent (peer-reviewed-preprint stage) work showing that alignment error is not fully removed by any filtering step and proposing to model the residual error inside the selection test instead of pretending it is gone. Useful for the 'honest limits' part of the plan: it establishes that even a best-practice PRANK + GUIDANCE pipeline leaves a residual false-positive floor, which is the correct framing for an undergraduate project claiming lineage-specific selection across 250 Myr. Pair it with the related caution on convergent-selection claims (bioRxiv 2021.10.26.465984, 'A cautionary tale on proper use of branch-site models to detect convergent positive selection') — directly relevant if the project wants to argue parrot/crocodilian convergence rather than simple lineage-specific change, since foreground-branch mislabelling and shared ancestral polymorphism both generate spurious convergence signals.

results.title: Green et al. 2014, Science — Three crocodilian genomes reveal ancestral patterns of evolution among archosaurs
results.snippet: The single strongest precedent for exactly what the user wants to do. Alligator mississippiensis, Crocodylus porosus and Gavialis gangeticus genomes analysed against birds; documents the very slow molecular rate in the crocodilian lineage (roughly an order of magnitude slower than birds/mammals) and — critically for angle (d) — uses that slow rate to computationally reconstruct a substantial fraction (~50%) of the common archosaurian ancestor's genome. It is the citable proof that ancestral-state reconstruction across the bird/croc split is a published, legitimate exercise, and it also defines the realistic ceiling: probable ancestral states and per-branch substitution counts, not a time-ordered mutational trajectory. Companion PDF is free at https://pgl.soe.ucsc.edu/green14.pdf.

results.title: St John et al. 2012, Genome Biology — Sequencing three crocodilian genomes to illuminate the evolution of archosaurs and amniotes
results.snippet: The project white paper for the crocodilian genomes, and the source to cite when calibrating the split. Verified quote: Crocodylomorpha 'appeared in the fossil record by the upper Triassic (about 200-250 Mya), a date coincident with molecular estimates of the avian-crocodilian divergence.' So '~250 Myr' is at the upper end of a defensible 200-250 Mya range rather than a point estimate — the user's framing needs softening to 'roughly 240-250 Myr (crown Archosauria; fossil minimum in the Late Triassic)'. Also sets out the taxonomic framing the project needs: extant crocodilians are crown Crocodylia within Crocodylomorpha, and Neosuchia is a much larger stem-inclusive clade, so 'Neosuchia' is the wrong label for the living comparator.

results.title: Irisarri et al. 2017, Nature Ecology & Evolution — Phylotranscriptomic consolidation of the jawed vertebrate timetree
results.snippet: The modern fossil-calibrated phylogenomic timetree to cite instead of TimeTree alone: 7,189 nuclear genes, 100 taxa, Bayesian relaxed-clock dating with explicit 95% credibility intervals for every amniote node including the bird/crocodilian split, and recovery of turtles as sister to Archosauria (which settles the outgroup choice for polarising changes). Pair it with the follow-up critique 'The Making of Calibration Sausage: Recalibrating the Transcriptomic Timetree of Jawed Vertebrates' (Front. Genet. 2021, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/genetics/articles/10.3389/fgene.2021.521693/full), which re-examines the same calibrations and shows how much the posterior ages move when the fossil priors are revised — the honest way to present a divergence date with uncertainty rather than a single number.

results.title: Williams, Pollock, Blackburne & Goldstein 2006, PLOS Comp Biol — Assessing the Accuracy of Ancestral Protein Reconstruction Methods
results.snippet: The foundational quantitative bias assessment and the single best citation for the epistemic-limits section. Verified figures: ML gives the most accurate per-site states yet its reconstructed ancestors are on average 1.5 +/- 1.6 kcal/mol too stable, MP 0.4 +/- 1.8, while Bayesian sampling from the posterior is essentially unbiased at 0.05 +/- 1.4. Mechanism is 'winner-takes-all': MP/ML pick the modal residue at every site and systematically delete the rarer, mildly destabilising variants that were really present, so small per-site errors accumulate into a large whole-sequence artefact. Direct consequence for the plan: never fold a single MAP ancestral sequence through the NIM AlphaFold/ESMFold endpoint and report its properties as the ancestor's — fold an ensemble sampled from the posterior.

results.title: Survivor bias drives overestimation of stability in reconstructed ancestral proteins (bioRxiv 2022)
results.snippet: The current form of the 'were ancient proteins really thermostable?' debate the angle asks for, and the counterweight to the Gaucher-style resurrection literature. Argues the high stability of reconstructed ancestors is largely an artefact of survivor bias plus the consensus effect: extant sequences are themselves a set filtered by selection against instability, so any consensus-like reconstruction inherits stabilising residues at each position, and the bias is compounded by uneven taxonomic sampling toward heavily sequenced clades. See also 'On the Potential Origins of the High Stability of Reconstructed Ancestral Proteins' (MBE 2016, https://academic.oup.com/mbe/article/33/10/2633/2925582). For this project: any claim that an ancestral archosaur protein was more stable or had a different pLDDT profile must be reported as possibly methodological, not biological.

results.title: Vialle, Tamuri & Goldman 2018, MBE — Alignment Modulates Ancestral Sequence Reconstruction Accuracy
results.snippet: Shows that the multiple-sequence alignment, not the ASR algorithm, is the dominant error source — the same reason PRANK vs MAFFT and trimAl/HmmCleaner filtering matter so much upstream, so this one paper anchors both angle (3) and angle (4). At a ~250 Myr divergence with saturated synonymous sites, alignment error is precisely the regime that manufactures both false positive branch-site selection hits and wrong ancestral states. Complement with the indel problem, which is the hardest limit on 'which mutations occurred': standard ML ASR has no indel model, so IQ-TREE --ancestral and FastML cannot honestly reconstruct gaps (see https://academic.oup.com/sysbio/article/72/2/307/6648472 for ARPIP and https://academic.oup.com/mbe/article/41/7/msae109/7688856 for indel-aware parsimony), and on the marginal-vs-joint choice, marginal is right for reporting one ancestral sequence while joint is required for counting substitutions along a branch (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13079920/) — neither recovers the temporal order of changes within a branch, which is simply not identifiable.

claims.claim: Multinucleotide mutations (MNMs) inflate the false-positive rate of the PAML codeml branch-site test far above its nominal level: in simulations with realistic MNM rates on the human lineage, 96% of genes exceeded a 5% false-positive rate at 5,000-codon alignment length, and in Drosophila almost 9% of genes were falsely called positively selected (vs ~1% in MNM-free control simulations).
claims.quote: At L= 5,000, 96% of human genes produced an unacceptable false positive rate (FPR >0.05) ... In flies, almost 9 percent of genes were falsely inferred to be under positive selection (P<0.05)

claims.claim: The branch-site test's positive-selection signal is driven overwhelmingly by codons with multiple differences (CMDs), which are the signature of MNMs: CMDs supply 60% (human) and 90% (fly) of the sites flagged as positively selected at posterior probability >0.9, despite being under 1% of all codons.
claims.quote: CMDs account for 60% and 90% of sites inferred a posteriori to have been positively selected (PP > 0.9) in humans and flies, respectively, although they represent <1% of all codons

claims.claim: In real genome-scale datasets (6,868 mammalian genes with complete coverage from 16,541 across six species; 8,564 genes across six Drosophila species) the number of genes called positively selected by the branch-site test is not greater than what MNM-induced bias alone would produce — i.e. the genome-wide selection scan is statistically indistinguishable from an artefact.
claims.quote: In both datasets, the number of genes that the BST infers to be positively selected does not exceed the number expected to be produced by MNM-induced bias alone.

claims.claim: The MNM bias is not confined to deeply diverged or saturated comparisons — it was observed across divergence levels from very low (human terminal branch) to moderate (Drosophila branches), so it cannot be dismissed as a deep-divergence-only problem in an archosaur-scale (bird vs crocodilian) branch-site analysis.
claims.quote: We observed strong bias on lineages with divergence levels ranging from very low (on the human terminal branch) to moderate (the fly branches), so this problem does not appear to be unique to highly diverged sequences.

claims.claim: The authors explicitly decline to endorse the MNM-aware branch-site model (BS+MNM) as a ready fix, stating more work is needed before it can be used with confidence, and recommend functional experimental validation rather than relying on the test alone — relevant because a purely in-silico project cannot supply that validation.
claims.quote: The BS+MNM test may be a promising means to accommodate MNMs, but there are many other forms of evolutionary complexity that are not incorporated into this model. More work is therefore required before the BS+MNM test or related techniques can be used with confidence.

claims.claim: Crocodilian beta-keratins are close enough to avian ones to serve as a working outgroup for avian beta-keratin phylogenies; the study used three named Crocodylus niloticus beta-keratin coding sequences (GenBank GI 215541571, 215541573, 187942180) to root a 222-taxon tree. This gives the parrot-vs-crocodilian project a published precedent and concrete accessions for polarising beta-keratin change across Archosauria.
claims.quote: As an outgroup for tree reconstruction, three β-keratin nucleotide coding sequences were used from Crocodylus niloticus (Nile crocodile) and were obtained via NCBI and have the following Genbank numbers: 215541571, 215541573 and 187942180

claims.claim: The inferred ancestral archosaurian genome contained a beta-keratin gene cluster closely related to present-day crocodilian scale beta-keratins, with avian scale genes basal within birds and claw genes basal to all feather and feather-like genes — i.e. feather keratins are a bird-lineage-specific duplication/divergence product, not an ancestral archosaur feature.
claims.quote: The genome of early archosaurians contained a cluster of β-keratin genes, closely related to the scale β-keratin genes seen in today's crocodilians and birds

claims.claim: Beta-keratin is a large, countable, chromosomally clustered multigene family in birds: 111 complete coding sequences in Gallus gallus and 108 in Taeniopygia guttata, with the claw/feather/feather-like/scale subfamilies in the same 5'-to-3' order on microchromosome 25 and large feather arrays on microchromosome 27 (61 probable genes in chicken, 41 in zebra finch). This makes copy-number expansion/contraction a tractable, falsifiable question for a Psittaciformes-vs-Crocodylia comparison.
claims.quote: We have identified a total of 111 complete β-keratin gene sequences (coding regions) in the G. gallus genome [7,8], which are distributed on three macrochromosomes (GGA1, 2 and 5), one intermediate chromosome (GGA6), two microchromosomes (GGA25, and 27), and "chromosome unknown" (GGA_Un)

claims.claim: The published analysis pipeline for this question is entirely CPU-light and reproducible on a workstation: tblastn/blastn gene mining with explicit E-value cut-offs (1e-10 for the permissive sweep), CLUSTAL W + PAL2NAL codon alignment, RAxML 7.0.3 with GTR+I+G and 1000 bootstraps, and PAML 4.0 site models M0/M1a/M2a/M3/M7/M8 validated by likelihood ratio tests against chi-square. No cluster, no GPU.
claims.quote: The large scale duplication seen among the feather β-keratin sequences were analyzed to determine amino acid sites under varying selective pressures using the PAML 4.0 package, in which six models of evolution were used [61]. Models tested were: M0 (one ratio), M1a (nearly neutral), M2a (positive selection), M3 (discrete), M7 (beta) and M8 (beta + ω).

claims.claim: Gene conversion and unequal crossing over are demonstrably active within this gene family (7 Bonferroni-significant shared fragments on chicken microchromosome 25, plus a 146-nt homogenised fragment between two zebra finch feather genes), which is a concrete confound for both dN/dS selection scans and ancestral state reconstruction in tandem arrays and must be tested with GENECONV before selection claims are made.
claims.quote: Seven fragments in our data set were found to be statistically significant and support the view that unequal crossing over has occurred on GGA25. Five of these fragments, which are 33 nucleotides long, were found between GGA25_Claw6 and GGA25_FK1, 7, 8, 10 and 12.

claims.claim: Single-best-state ancestral sequence reconstruction is highly accurate at the per-site level in simulation — roughly 90-94% of sites across all internal nodes are recovered correctly — with maximum likelihood (93.7 ± 4.5%) slightly beating Bayesian inference (92.3 ± 5.2%) and both beating maximum parsimony (89.8 ± 6.9%). This supports reporting ASR site-by-site accuracy but also means ~6-10% of reconstructed sites are wrong even under a correctly specified model.
claims.quote: 93.7 ± 4.5% of all nodes at all sites correctly reconstructed

claims.claim: ML and MP ancestral reconstructions are systematically biased toward hyper-stable (consensus-like) sequences: reconstructed ancestors have folding free energies too negative by 1.5 ± 1.6 kcal/mol (ML) and 0.4 ± 1.8 kcal/mol (MP). Bayesian sampling of ancestral states largely removes this bias (0.05 ± 1.4 kcal/mol). Any claim that a reconstructed archosaur ancestral protein was unusually thermostable must therefore be treated as a possible methodological artefact, not a biological result.
claims.quote: ΔG_Folding for BI reconstructions are on average only 0.05 ± 1.4 kcal/mol too negative

claims.claim: The stability/consensus bias in ML reconstruction grows worse with node depth (correlation −0.61, p = 0.02), whereas Bayesian inference shows no significant correlation with depth. For a ~240-255 Myr archosaur split, where the nodes of interest are the deepest in the tree, this is precisely the regime in which ML point-estimate ancestors are most biased — favouring Bayesian/sampled ancestral states over single ML best-state sequences.
claims.quote: statistically significant increase in reconstruction bias with the depth

claims.claim: The mechanism of the bias is that ML and parsimony assign the single most probable/most favourable amino acid at each site, discarding the less-favourable variants that segregate in real populations; the reconstructed ancestor is therefore a composite that may never have existed as a real historical sequence. This directly bounds what 'projecting the mutations of the last 250 Myr' can claim: a most-probable composite state per node, not an actual ancestral individual's sequence.
claims.quote: usually assign to the ancestor the most favourable amino acids

claims.claim: The comparison is a controlled simulation study under a known true history (simulated protein evolution with an explicit thermodynamic fitness model), so the reported accuracy figures are upper bounds obtained with the generating model known; real-data reconstructions with model misspecification, alignment error and unknown topology will be less accurate than 93.7%.
claims.quote: 93.7 ± 4.5% of all nodes at all sites correctly reconstructed

claims.claim: In codon-level simulations spanning a wide range of divergence levels and indel rates, choice of multiple sequence aligner is the dominant determinant of false positives in sitewise positive-selection tests: PRANK's codon-aware alignments were the most accurate and ClustalW the least, so a codon-aware aligner (PRANK/PRANK-C, or MACSE/PAL2NAL-style codon alignment) should be used upstream of PAML/HyPhy rather than a default protein or DNA aligner.
claims.quote: We found that some aligners led to many false positives, whereas others resulted in very few. ... Of the aligners tested, PRANK's codon-based alignments consistently performed the best and ClustalW performed the worst.

claims.claim: Alignment filtering is not a general remedy: of the filters tested GUIDANCE was best and Gblocks worst, and no filter substantially improved PRANK alignments under most conditions — so routinely applying Gblocks/trimAl on top of a good codon alignment adds trimming cost without reducing false-positive selection calls.
claims.quote: Of the filters tested, GUIDANCE performed the best and Gblocks performed the worst. Although some filters showed good ability to reduce the error rates from ClustalW and MAFFT alignments, none were found to substantially improve the performance of PRANK alignments under most conditions.

claims.claim: At deep divergence the dominant error mode flips from false positives to false negatives: false negatives affected every aligner and grew with sequence divergence, meaning a bird-vs-crocodilian (~240-255 Myr) selection scan will systematically under-detect truly selected sites, and a negative result is weak evidence of no selection.
claims.quote: False negatives were a problem for all aligners, increasing with sequence divergence. ... Controls using the true alignment and an optimal filtering method suggested that performance improvements could be gained by improving aligners or filters to reduce the prevalence of false negatives, especially at higher divergence levels and indel rates.

claims.claim: Low false-positive rates in sitewise selection tests are achievable even for extremely divergent, indel-rich sequences provided the best aligner is used — i.e. deep archosaur divergence does not by itself invalidate sitewise dN/dS scans, it shifts the risk to power loss.
claims.quote: With the best aligner, a low false positive rate was maintained even with extremely divergent indel-prone sequences.

claims.claim: The prevalence of misalignment-driven errors and the mitigating power of filters were, as of 2012, not well characterised despite filters being applied as routine practice — so a project that cites 'we ran Gblocks' as its safeguard against alignment-driven false positives is invoking an untested convention rather than a validated control.
claims.quote: When detecting positive selection in proteins, the prevalence of errors resulting from misalignment and the ability of alignment filters to mitigate such errors are not well understood, but filters are commonly applied to try to avoid false positive results.

claims.claim: Ancestral sequence reconstruction carries a systematic, method-wide bias toward reconstructing ancestors LONGER than the true ancestor, caused by a preference for inferring insertions over deletions; this affects nearly all MSA pipelines, and only PRANK variants (PRANK*, PRANK+F, PRANK+F*) balanced indels well enough to recover approximately correct ancestral length.
claims.quote: We also discover a bias towards reconstructed sequences longer than the true ancestors, deriving from a preference for inferring insertions, in almost all MSA methodological approaches.

claims.claim: ASR accuracy degrades sharply with increasing evolutionary divergence (tree height) — in the hardest simulated scenario (64 taxa, tree height 2.0, sampling fraction 0.01, indel rate 0.05) reconstruction accuracy fell below 0.3 for every alignment method tested. This directly bounds what can be claimed about ancestral archosaur sequences across a ~240-255 Myr divergence.
claims.quote: Tree height is also a critical variable, with longer trees (more divergent sequences) presenting more difficult scenarios and lower reconstruction accuracies.

claims.claim: The choice of aligner is not neutral for ASR: MAFFT consistency modes (E-INS-i, L-INS-i) and PRANK variants give the best reconstruction accuracy, while FSA performs worst (insertion error exceeding 0.8, i.e. ~80% of the alignment being gaps relative to the true sequence) — so a default MAFFT FFT-NS-2 or MUSCLE run is a materially inferior upstream choice.
claims.quote: The MAFFT consistency aligners and PRANK variants exhibit the best performance, whereas FSA displays limited performance.

claims.claim: Denser taxon sampling near the node of interest improves ASR accuracy: reconstructions of later (shallower) divergences are markedly more accurate, and adding extant taxa gives a modest accuracy gain — arguing for sampling many Psittaciformes and many Crocodylia plus outgroups rather than one genome per clade.
claims.quote: The sampling fraction drastically affects accuracy, with a higher fraction (later divergences) yielding more accurate reconstructions.

claims.claim: Alignment quality can be used as a diagnostic proxy for reconstruction reliability: MSA quality scores correlated with ASR accuracy with coefficients of determination typically above 0.75, so alignment-quality filtering is a defensible pre-registered QC gate before any ancestral-state claim.

claims.claim: Ancestral sequences and consensus sequences derived from populations that evolved under selection for stability are systematically biased toward thermostability, meaning high measured stability of a reconstructed ancestor is not by itself evidence that the real ancestral protein (or its environment) was thermostable/hot.
claims.quote: We show that ancestors and consensus sequences derived from populations evolved under selective pressure for stability throughout their history are significantly biased toward thermostability.

claims.claim: The authors propose 'survivor bias' as a mechanism distinct from and complementary to the previously invoked 'consensus bias': because thermodynamically unstable proteins are purged by selection, the extant sequence alignment that ASR is built from is already enriched for stabilising amino acids at each position, so alignment-based reconstruction inherits that enrichment.
claims.quote: As thermodynamically unstable proteins will be selected against, ancestral or consensus sequences derived from extant sequences are selected from a dataset biased towards the more stabilising amino acids in each position.

claims.claim: The conclusion is derived from a simulation study — a parameterizable in silico model of protein evolution tracking stability at population, protein and amino-acid levels — not from experimental resurrection of real ancestral proteins, so it demonstrates that the bias is expected under plausible evolutionary models rather than measuring its magnitude in any specific empirical ASR dataset.
claims.quote: We thoroughly explore the presence of survivor bias using a highly parameterizable in silico model of protein evolution that tracks stability at the population, protein, and amino acid levels.

claims.claim: Reconstructed thermostable ancestors have been reported for proteins from lineages known to have evolved at moderate temperatures, which is inconsistent with reading ASR thermostability as a direct record of ancient environmental temperature (the 'hot-start' inference).
claims.quote: Many ancestral sequences are thermostable, supporting the "hot-start" hypothesis for lifes origin. Recent studies have observed thermostable ancient proteins that evolved in moderate temperatures.

claims.claim: The paper frames its output as methodological guidance for ASR practice — i.e. that conclusions drawn from reconstructed ancestors require explicit control for reconstruction bias — which for an archosaur ASR project means biophysical properties of predicted ancestral parrot/crocodilian proteins must be reported as bias-prone inferences rather than as ancestral phenotype.
claims.quote: It provides guidance for the thorough derivation of conclusions from future ancestral sequence reconstruction work.

claims.claim: The Amazona aestiva reference assembly (Aaes1) published in this paper is scaffold-level and fragmentary by modern standards: 120.6x coverage, 3,232 scaffolds, scaffold N50 1.09 Mb, contig N50 only 27.8 kb — and it was nonetheless the most contiguous parrot genome as of 2018. Any project using 2018-era Amazona/macaw/kea assemblies inherits contig N50s in the tens of kb, which is inadequate for whole-genome alignment or synteny; the VGP/B10K chromosome-level replacements are required instead.
claims.quote: The resultant assembly (Aaes1) contains 3,232 scaffolds with a scaffold N50 size of 1.09 Mb and a contig N50 size of 27.8 kb, surpassing all previous parrot genome assemblies in sequence contiguity

claims.claim: The published precedent for parrot-lineage selection analysis used exactly the tool chain proposed for this project and at a scale that fits 15 GB RAM: OrthoMCL clustering of proteins from 23 annotated bird genomes yielded 22,380 clusters, of which 4,132 were strict single-copy orthologs; codon alignments were built with PRANK and dN/dS was tested with PAML codeml (null model=0 vs alternative model=2, i.e. the two-ratio BRANCH model despite being described as 'branch-sites'), recovering 344 genes (8%) with differential omega between high- and regular-longevity birds.
claims.quote: Of these, 4,132 represented single-gene ortholog clusters (SGOs), with no more than one copy in each of the 23 bird species. In order to infer the level of selective pressure acting on longevity gene sets, phylogenetically-aware CDS alignments were generated by PRANK (), rooted with a tree obtained from the Avian Phylogenomics data []. To assess ratios of nonsynonymous (Ka) to synonymous (Ks) substitution rates we implemented branch-sites test of selection using codeml from the PAML (Phylogenetic Analysis by Maximum Likelihood) package

claims.claim: This paper's genome-wide selection scan applied an uncorrected raw likelihood-ratio-test threshold of p < 0.01 across all 4,132 orthologs, with no FDR or Bonferroni correction reported anywhere in the STAR Methods or the Quantification and Statistical Analysis section; at 4,132 tests an uncorrected alpha of 0.01 expects ~41 false positives, so the '344 genes under selection' figure is not multiple-testing corrected. A student replicating this design must add BH-FDR rather than copy the published threshold.
claims.quote: To identify genes under selection in HL birds relative to RL birds, null versus alternate models of selection were compared using a likelihood ratio test (LRT, p-value < 0.01, degrees of freedom = 1). To identify specific codon sites under selection in HL birds, a LRT was used to compare the likelihood values of a neutral agains a positive selection model (p-value < 0.01, degrees of freedom = 2; posterior probabilities of positively selected sites were estimated with Bayes Empirical Bayes with α = 0.05).

claims.claim: Crocodilian genomes are an established outgroup in parrot comparative genomics: American alligator was used alongside anole lizard and human as the non-avian outgroup panel for cross-species BLAT validation of parrot-specific novel genes. This is direct published precedent for the archosaur-scale bird-vs-crocodilian comparison, and it shows the outgroup role (polarising presence/absence) rather than a pairwise whole-genome alignment role.
claims.quote: those predictions that were not excluded through the BLAST alignment were aligned to two distantly related parrot species (budgerigar, Kea) and outgroup species (zebra finch, Peregrine Falcon, chicken, American alligator, Anole lizard, and human) using BLAT with sensitized parameters optimized for these cross-species alignments, in order to confirm the presence of orthologous novel genes in all parrots and absence in non-parrots

claims.claim: Assembly fragmentation, not method choice, was the binding limit on orthology inference: the authors state that the Kea, Scarlet Macaw and Puerto Rican Parrot assemblies were too fragmentary for the manual synteny verification they consider necessary for correct orthology calls, and they treat synteny verification (not reciprocal BLAST/BLAT alone) as the step that discriminates paralogs from orthologs. This bears directly on whether the project should invest in synteny tools (MCScanX/GENESPACE) versus reciprocal-best-hit approaches.
claims.quote: We were unable to distinguish these possibilities, due to the fragmentary nature of the current Kea, Scarlet Macaw, and Puerto Rican Parrot assemblies, which precludes the syntenic analysis necessary for accurate orthology determination.

claims.claim: Across coding alignments of 7,986 orthologous genes from 47 avian genomes (Jarvis et al. dataset), dN/dS computed over ALL substitutions shows no significant correlation with life-history traits, but dN/dS restricted to GC-conservative substitutions (S-to-S plus W-to-W, i.e. the classes unaffected by GC-biased gene conversion) recovers strong positive correlations with body mass, age of sexual maturity and longevity. Practical consequence for a parrot-vs-crocodilian scan: naive genome-wide dN/dS in birds is a biased estimator of the efficacy of selection, and the fix is to partition substitutions by GC class, not merely to add more genes. [The extractor stripped italicised 'dN/dS' and 'Ne' symbols from the HTML, producing the glued words in the quote.]
claims.quote: By estimating nucleotide substitution rates separately for different substitution categories, we observe strong positive correlations between three life-history traits (body mass, age of sexual maturity and longevity) andwhen the estimation ofis based on GC-conservative substitutions only. No significant correlations were observed when estimation ofwas based on all substitutions together, which can be ascribed to the influence of gBGC on S-to-W or W-to-S substitutions.

claims.claim: The direction of the gBGC bias on dN/dS is lineage-specific: it deflates dN/dS in most avian lineages but inflates it in others, because the net effect depends on the lineage's equilibrium GC content (GC*) minus its ancestral GC content (deltaGC), which the authors measured as differing between synonymous and non-synonymous sites (deltaGC_syn = 0.076 +/- 0.071 vs deltaGC_nonsyn = 0.026 +/- 0.038). This means a lineage-specific (branch or branch-site) test on a parrot branch versus a crocodilian branch can be biased in opposite directions on the two branches, manufacturing an apparent rate shift with no selective cause.
claims.quote: The impact of gBGC onvaries substantially among lineages, where it increases theratio in some lineages, but decreases it in others. Our analysis suggests that these contrasting effects are related to differences in the dynamics of base composition between non-synonymous and synonymous substitutions.

claims.claim: Alignment cleaning and gene-set choice do NOT rescue the biased inference: the authors re-analysed two previously published, independently filtered avian alignment sets (Figuet et al. + HMMcleaner, and Botero-Castro et al. with 1,245 extra GC-rich genes) and the failure persisted in every set unless gBGC was explicitly accounted for. So HmmCleaner/Gblocks/trimAl-style filtering upstream is necessary but demonstrably not sufficient to make avian dN/dS trustworthy.
claims.quote: Taken together, the hypothesis that gBGC conceals the prediction of the nearly neutral theory appears robust to the set of genes analyzed as well as to alignment quality.based on GC-conservative changes showed strong positive correlations with all life-history traits analyzed in this study in all datasets, while correlations were weak when analyzing all substitutions together. This demonstrates that gene set and alignment quality alone do not explain the lack of a positive correlation between life-history traits andin birds.

claims.claim: The authors explicitly state that published conclusions which ignored gBGC need re-evaluation, and they supply a concrete software protocol to do so: the Bio++ toolchain (bppml to fit a NON-STATIONARY homogeneous codon model — YN98/F3X4, T92X3 or L95X3 — then MapNH for substitution mapping to get dN and dS per branch per substitution category, and bppancestor for ancestral sequence reconstruction at internal nodes). This is a named, installable CLI alternative/complement to PAML codeml and HyPhy for this project, and bppancestor is directly relevant to the ancestral-state-reconstruction angle.
claims.quote: As a first step, we used a non-stationary homogeneous codon model of molecular evolution implemented in bppml to retrieve the most likely branch lengths, codon frequencies at the root, and substitution model parameters. We implemented three different substitution models, which all allow for different GC content dynamics between codon positions, YN98 (F3X4) [], T92X3 [], and L95X3 []. As a second step, we used MapNH for substitution mapping to estimateand, and then... To reconstruct the most likely ancestral sequence at each node, we used the bppancestor program

claims.claim: dN/dS estimates in birds are additionally confounded by local GC content and chromosome size independently of gBGC: values are systematically lower for GC-rich genes and for genes on microchromosomes (<16 Mb, chr14-28) than for GC-poor genes and macrochromosomes (>100 Mb, chr1-3), and this reduction persists even within the GC-conservative substitution class. Because avian microchromosomes have no equivalent in crocodilian karyotypes, a bird-vs-crocodilian dN/dS comparison must stratify by chromosome class/GC content or it will confound genome architecture with selection.
claims.quote: Estimates ofwere lower for genes with higher GC content and for genes located in microchromosomes. This reduction appears to be unrelated to gBGC, as it is observed for all substitution categories including GC-conservative substitutions.

claims.claim: Irisarri et al. date the origins of the main sauropsid lineages — including the crocodile/bird (Archosauria) split — to the Permian, in a band from ~294 Mya (95% CrI 313–273) to ~259 Mya (CrI 288–226). This places the bird–crocodilian divergence at or before ~250–260 Mya rather than the commonly quoted 240 Myr, and the credibility intervals are wide (up to ~60 Myr), so the project should state the split as roughly 250–290 Mya with explicit uncertainty rather than a point value of '250 million years'.
claims.quote: The origins of the main sauropsid groups, i.e., turtles, crocodiles, birds, squamates and tuatara ( Sphenodon ), took place in the Permian from 294 (313–273) to 259 (288–226) Mya.

claims.claim: The genome-wide divergence times were obtained by averaging 100 timetrees estimated from independent gene jackknife replicates of ~15,000 amino acids each, under a CAT-GTR+Γ substitution model and an autocorrelated lognormal relaxed clock in PhyloBayes, with 95% credibility intervals taken as the absolute max/min across the 100 replicates — i.e. dating a deep divergence credibly requires Bayesian relaxed-clock inference over many independent gene subsamples, not a single concatenated run.
claims.quote: We applied an auto-correlated lognormal relaxed clock model and best-fitting sequence evolution model (CAT-GTR) to estimate genome-wide divergence times, averaged over 100 gene jackknife replicates.

claims.claim: Fossil-calibration choice materially changes the resulting ages: two cross-validated calibration schemes (C16 with 16 calibrations, C30 with 30) produced 'largely congruent' but node-specific differences, with C30 overestimating ages within turtles, frogs and neoavian birds and underestimating iguanian squamates and snakes. Calibration cross-validation (removing poorly performing calibrations one at a time) is therefore a required step, and any single published divergence date is conditional on its calibration set.
claims.quote: Both schemes produced largely congruent divergence times, but C16 yielded more reasonable dates within turtles, frogs, neoavian birds, modern frogs (overestimated in C30 if compared with previous data; www.timetree.org ) or iguanian squamates and snakes (underestimated in C30)

claims.claim: Turtles (Testudines) are recovered as the sister group of crocodiles plus birds (Archosauria) with maximal support, and topology tests statistically rejected both the anapsid placement of turtles and a turtle+crocodile or turtle+lepidosaur grouping. This fixes the correct outgroup structure for polarising parrot-vs-crocodilian changes: a testudine is the nearest outgroup to Archosauria, with Lepidosauria (squamates/Sphenodon) and Mammalia as successively more distant outgroups.
claims.quote: Turtles were the sister group of crocodiles and birds (Archosauria), in agreement with the majority of previous phylogenomic studies 10 , 11 and the latest morphological evidence 36 . Topology tests rejected the traditional view of turtles as primarily anapsids (early-branching within "reptiles") as well as possible sister-group with either lepidosaurians or crocodiles

claims.claim: Mitochondrial genomes are explicitly judged insufficient to resolve the deepest gnathostome relationships because of limited signal and among-lineage rate heterogeneity; the robust result required 7,189 nuclear genes (3,791,500 aligned amino acid positions) from 100 taxa. A parrot-vs-crocodilian deep-divergence analysis should therefore be built on large nuclear ortholog sets, not mitogenomes.
claims.quote: We reconstruct a robust and strongly supported timetree of jawed vertebrates using 7,189 nuclear genes from 100 taxa, including 23 new transcriptomes from previously unsampled key species. ... Mitochondrial genomes prove insufficient to resolve the deepest relationships because of limited signal and among-lineage rate heterogeneity.

input.summary: The verified evidence establishes a solid data foundation and one hard compute constraint, but covers only part of the research question. On data: chromosome-level, RefSeq-annotated reference genomes exist for both anchor species — Melopsittacus undulatus GCF_012275295.1 (bMelUnd1.mat.Z, VGP/B10K, 1.17 Gb, 32 chromosomes, scaffold N50 104.1 Mb, annotation RS_2024_11 with 16,457 protein-coding genes) and Alligator mississippiensis GCF_030867095.1 (rAllMis1, VGP, 2.35 Gb, 16 chromosomes, scaffold N50 255.1 Mb, annotation RS_2023_09 with 20,269 protein-coding genes) — so the project can start from ready-made CDS/protein FASTA (~43 MB per species) with no de novo annotation. On method: Progressive Cactus is confirmed out of reach on the 20-core/15 GB WSL2 box — official Cactus docs provision 208-416 GiB per alignment job, the Harvard FAS sauropsid pipeline requires a SLURM cluster, and the 605-genome amniote alignment consumed hundreds of 32-vCPU AWS nodes — so the pairwise bird-vs-crocodilian WGA must go through LASTZ chain/net, minimap2 asm20, or nf-core/pairgenomealign. On epistemics: the Cactus authors themselves state ancestral genome reconstructions are "only a hypothetical reconstruction of the true history", which is the citable anchor for honestly bounding the user's "250 Myr of mutations" framing. Critically, the third comparator is a trap: the gharial RefSeq reference GCF_001723915.1 advertises a 96.08 Mb scaffold N50 that is a Ragout reference-guided artefact over a real contig N50 of 14,799 bp. No claim about molecular dating, clade naming (Neosuchia vs Crocodylia), PAML/HyPhy failure modes, orthology tools, or candidate gene-family research questions survived verification, so angles 3, 4 (dating half) and 5 of the brief remain unevidenced here.

findings.claim: The Cactus authors themselves supply the citable epistemic caveat for the user's core question: ancestral genome reconstructions are 'only a hypothetical reconstruction of the true history', not a historical record — and the caveat attaches specifically to the inferred per-branch substitution/indel/rearrangement history the user wants to project over 250 Myr.

findings.evidence: Armstrong et al. 2020, Nature 587:246-251, doi:10.1038/s41586-020-2871-y, verbatim: 'Although this history is by its nature only a hypothetical reconstruction of the true history of genome evolution along the tree, it is accurate enough to be useful.' The antecedent sentence pins what 'this history' means: 'The ancestral reconstructions provide a history of substitution, indel, and rearrangement events.' The sentence sits in the 600-way AMNIOTE alignment section — the exact taxonomic scope of a parrot-vs-crocodilian project. The bioRxiv v3 preprint carries the same wording ('by and large accurate enough to be useful'), confirming no paraphrase drift. The two-clause structure must be preserved in the write-up: the caveat is 'hypothetical BUT useful', not a blanket dismissal. A search for critiques found nothing disputing the caveat; the literature only sharpens it in the same direction (accuracy degrades with divergence; uncertain sites are non-randomly distributed, cf. Genetics 221:iyac074 on the LINE-1 progenitor; progressive alignment depends on guide-tree accuracy). IMPORTANT SCOPE LIMIT — do not over-cite this one sentence: it covers whole-genome ancestral SEQUENCE/rearrangement reconstruction from alignment. It does NOT cover (a) codon-level ASR with PAML/IQ-TREE/FastML, (b) the documented reconstruction bias toward consensus/thermostable ancestral sequences, or (c) the separate and stronger limitation that the temporal ORDER of substitutions within a branch is unidentifiable. Those need their own citations, which this research round did not verify. Not time-expired: Progressive Cactus/HAL remains the standard deep-divergence aligner (Zoonomia, VGP, B10K) as of 2026, and epistemic limits have no shelf life.
