results.title: Xia et al. 2024, Nature — On the genetic basis of tail-loss evolution in humans and apes
results.snippet: THE primary source (PMID 38418917, PMC10901737, Nature 626:1042-1048). Exact claim: an AluY in TBXT intron 6 pairs in reverse orientation with an ancestral AluSx1 in intron 5, forming a stem-loop that skips exon 6 → hominoid-specific TBXT^Δexon6 isoform. Model organism is MOUSE, not ape. Four alleles: Tbxt^Δexon6/+, Tbxt^insASAY (the actual human Alu pair), Tbxt^insRCS2 (synthetic 220 bp inverted repeat), Tbxt^insRCS2/Δexon6. Penetrance: Tbxt^Δexon6/+ = 21/63 (33%) affected (4 no tail, 9 short, 8 kinked), 0/35 in WT littermates; Tbxt^insRCS2/insRCS2 ≈ 10% shorter tail; Tbxt^insRCS2/Δexon6 = 19/19 complete tail absence. Phenotype scales with the Δexon6 : full-length isoform ratio in the E10.5 tailbud. NTD cost: spina-bifida-like neural tube closure defects in Tbxt^Δexon6/Δexon6 HOMOZYGOTES only, with just 2 documented cases plus E9 arrest / E11.5 malformation with death at birth — the '1 in 1,000 neonates' figure is imported human epidemiology, not a measured model penetrance. CAVEAT the authors themselves state: Tbxt^insASAY, the only allele carrying the genuine human sequence, did NOT produce high Δexon6 in the embryonic tailbud (worked only in ES cells), so sufficiency of the Alu pair in vivo is explicitly 'inconclusive'; the tail phenotype came from engineered surrogate alleles. FLAGS for the avian question: (1) single non-replicated study; (2) Alu is a primate-specific SINE — birds have CR1 LINEs and no active SINE family, so this exact mechanism was unavailable to the avian stem lineage; (3) zero avian data in the paper; (4) sign error for the parent's design — this shows a single lesion SHORTENS a tail via a dominant-interfering isoform, not that removing one lengthens it.

results.title: Xia et al. 2021, bioRxiv preprint — The genetic basis of tail-loss evolution in humans and apes
results.snippet: The 2021 preprint (Europe PMC PPR395284; mirrored at Research Square 10.21203/rs.3.rs-907475/v1) of the Nature paper. Useful as a provenance check on how the claim tightened through peer review: the preprint described a SINGLE mouse model, said tail loss occurred 'albeit with incomplete penetrance', and described the homozygous phenotype as 'embryonic spinal cord malformations, resembling a neural tube defect condition'. The published version added the insASAY/insRCS2 allelic series and the isoform-ratio dose argument. Comparing the two versions is the cleanest way to see which parts of the tail-loss/NTD trade-off are data and which are framing — the trade-off claim is worded as a proposal ('we propose that selection... was associated with an adaptive cost') in both.

results.title: Denisko et al. 2026, Nucleic Acids Research — Inverted Alu repeats in loop-out exon skipping across hominoid evolution
results.snippet: Independent, genome-wide generalization of the exact mechanism Xia et al. invoked (PMID 41883293; preprint 10.1101/2025.03.07.642063). Shows inverted Alu pairs — notably AluY–AluSx1, the same subfamily pairing as at TBXT — are enriched flanking skippable exons genome-wide, predicted to form stable stem-loops, and that exons with weak 3' acceptor sites are most susceptible; identifies 67,126 hominoid-specific Alu insertions across nine primates with experimental validation of several. This substantially de-risks the MECHANISTIC half of Xia et al. (the loop-out splicing is real and general) while sharpening the transfer problem: the mechanism is intrinsically Alu-dependent and therefore primate-restricted. For the avian design this is the decisive negative — any engineered inverted-repeat exon-skip in Gallus would have to be built de novo from synthetic sequence (as Xia's own insRCS2 allele was), not borrowed from an endogenous avian repeat family.

results.title: Li et al. 2026, Animal Genetics — Haplotype variation of TBXT enhancer contributes to tail length diversity of sheep
results.snippet: The most transferable piece of the TBXT story for a non-primate amniote (PMID 41902793). The T-bound notochord enhancer (TNE) is a CONSERVED VERTEBRATE cis-regulatory element governing TBXT expression in tailbud patterning and notochord formation — it has an avian ortholog, unlike Alu. 575 sheep across five tail morphotypes: oTNE haplotype H001 dominates tailless fat-rumped breeds, H002/H003 dominate long-tailed breeds; validated in a segregating F2 (n=79, Texel × Kazakh) by X-ray caudal vertebral counts, with luciferase assays showing H001 has significantly higher enhancer activity and the enhancer carrying a T-box motif enabling TBXT autoregulation. Demonstrates a purely cis-regulatory, non-coding lesion tuning caudal vertebral number in a second mammalian lineage — i.e. a regulatory handle on tail length that could in principle be interrogated in chicken. Caveat: association + reporter assay, no in vivo genome edit; and enhancer activity direction (higher activity in the TAILLESS haplotype) is counterintuitive and unreplicated.

results.title: Su et al. 2024, Gene — Short-tailed phenotype from TBXT c.G334T CRISPR mouse model
results.snippet: A coding-lesion alternative to the Xia splicing route (PMID 38401832). CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in of the sheep-derived TBXT c.G334T point mutation into mouse produces a short-tail phenotype, and the authors link it to altered Wnt pathway output — Axin2, Dkk1, Wnt3, Wnt3a and Wnt5a all significantly differ between mutant and wild-type embryos across developmental stages. Relevant two ways: it independently confirms that TBXT dosage/function is a rate-limiting node for caudal extension in amniotes via a completely different molecular lesion (missense, not exon skip), and it ties TBXT directly to WNT3A — the same axis as the vestigial-tail mouse the parent brief asks about. Flag: single-lab study, mouse only, expression-level mechanism rather than epistasis experiments; the Wnt regulatory-network claim is correlative.

results.title: Wang et al. 2025, Life — TBXT and Brachyury protein differentially expressed during early embryonic development of Hu and Hulunbuir sheep
results.snippet: Spatiotemporal FISH/immunofluorescence comparison of TBXT mRNA and Brachyury protein between a long-tailed (Hu) and short-tailed (Hulunbuir) sheep breed at E16 and E19 (PMID 41157233). Included only as the descriptive expression counterpart to the sheep genetic work: at E19 TBXT is concentrated in tailbud in both breeds but with breed-specific differences in limb ectoderm vs midgut, and Brachyury protein localizes to tailbud in Hu but heart/hindgut in Hulunbuir. Weak evidence — different embryonic ages compared between breeds (16 d vs 19 d), no quantification, no genotype linkage, and the abstract slips between sheep and goat. Useful only to note that breed-level tail differences show up as tailbud TBXT expression differences, not as gene loss.

claims.claim: In mouse, progressive reduction of Cdx dosage (an allelic series of Cdx1/Cdx2/Cdx4 mutants) produces progressively more severe posterior vertebral truncation, and Cdx2+/-;Cdx4-/- compound mutants fail to generate any posterior tissue caudal to the hindlimbs — establishing Cdx dosage as a quantitative dial on axial extension length. This is a pure mouse result; the paper presents no avian data, so transfer to the chicken caudal program is unvalidated.
claims.quote: Decrease in Cdx dosage in an allelic series of mouse Cdx mutants leads to progressively more severe posterior vertebral defects. ... Compound mutants carrying one Cdx2 null allele and homozygous null for Cdx4...fail to generate their posterior tissues caudal to the hindlimbs.

claims.claim: Precocious/premature expression of HOX paralogous group 13 genes truncates the vertebral axis in mouse by antagonizing Cdx function, i.e. HOX13 acts as a terminator of axial extension operating through the Cdx node rather than in a parallel pathway — the phenotype phenocopies loss of Cdx activity.
claims.quote: Precocious expression of Hox paralogous 13 genes also induces vertebral axis truncation by antagonizing Cdx function. ... Premature expression of Hox13 genes thus leads to a phenotype similar to that resulting from a decrease in Cdx activity

claims.claim: Posterior gain of function of the canonical Wnt effector Lef1 rescues the posterior vertebral defects caused by reduced Cdx dosage, placing Cdx downstream of / integrated with canonical Wnt signalling in a single Cdx-Wnt network whose site of action is the posterior growth zone of the tail bud.
claims.quote: These defects are corrected by posterior gain of function of the Wnt effector Lef1. ... We propose that the site of action of this network centered on Cdx and Wnt resides in the posterior growth zone in the tail bud, and reveals a unifying function of Cdx genes in posterior morphogenesis of tissues in the three germ layers.

claims.claim: Wnt3a hypomorphic alleles produce a graded vertebral truncation series intermediate between Wnt3a-null and mild hypomorph phenotypes, showing that tail length in mouse is sensitive to WNT3A signalling level rather than to its presence/absence alone — consistent with a regulatory (dosage) rather than gene-loss route to tail shortening.
claims.quote: Wnt3a hypomorph mutants...exhibit a vertebral truncation phenotype of intermediate severity between the Wnt3a-null mutants...and the mild Wnt3a hypomorph mutants.

claims.claim: Reduced Cdx dosage also causes caudal neural tube malformation (ectopic ventral neural structures, aberrant neurepithelial morphogenesis) alongside axial truncation, indicating that axis-shortening manipulations at the tailbud growth zone carry neural tube cost as a coupled phenotype — the same class of cost reported for TBXT-mediated hominoid tail loss.
claims.quote: Ventral ectopic neural structures (ens) were also found in Cdx2 null...and in Cdx2/4 double null mutant embryos.

claims.claim: Homozygous Hoxb13 loss-of-function mice show overgrowth of every major tail-bud-derived structure — secondary neural tube, caudal spinal ganglia, and caudal vertebrae — establishing HOXB13 as a terminator/repressor of caudal axial growth in mouse (this is the 'longer tail' Hoxb13-null phenotype).
claims.quote: Mice homozygous for Hoxb13 loss-of-function mutations show overgrowth in all major structures derived from the tail bud, including the developing secondary neural tube (SNT), the caudal spinal ganglia, and the caudal vertebrae.

claims.claim: The mechanism of the Hoxb13-null tail overgrowth is cell-behavioral rather than patterning: increased cell proliferation together with decreased apoptosis in the tail — i.e. wild-type HOXB13 normally promotes programmed cell death in the tail bud. This is directly relevant to whether distal caudal somite elimination by apoptosis is a conserved amniote mechanism.
claims.quote: These phenotypes can be explained by the observed increased cell proliferation and decreased levels of apoptosis within the tail of homozygous mutant mice.

claims.claim: The authors assign HOXB13 three separable proposed functions — inhibitor of neuronal proliferation, activator of apoptosis in the secondary neural tube, and general growth repressor in caudal vertebrae — but frame these as a suggestion inferred from the phenotype, not as demonstrated molecular mechanism (no target genes or apoptotic pathway components identified in the abstract).
claims.quote: This analysis of Hoxb13 function suggests that this 5' Hox gene may act as an inhibitor of neuronal cell proliferation, an activator of apoptotic pathways in the SNT, and as a general repressor of growth in the caudal vertebrae.

claims.claim: Hoxb13 expression (mapped with a beta-galactosidase knock-in reporter that is itself a loss-of-function allele) is in the developing spinal cord and caudal mesoderm, spatially coincident with the tissues that overgrow in mutants — so the reporter cannot report expression in a genetically wild-type background, a caveat on the expression/phenotype correlation.
claims.quote: Using the beta-galactosidase reporter allele of Hoxb13, also a loss-of-function allele, we found that the expression patterns of Hoxb13 in the developing spinal cord and caudal mesoderm are closely associated with overgrowth phenotypes in the tails of homozygous mutant animals.

claims.claim: All evidence in this paper is from targeted mouse alleles (Mus musculus); the study contains no chicken, avian, or other non-mammalian data, so any use of HOXB13 as a candidate terminator of avian axial elongation is a mouse-to-bird extrapolation not tested here. Note also that birds lack an HOXB13 orthologue in the canonical HoxB cluster annotation, which makes the transfer weaker still and must be checked against a current galliform assembly rather than this 2003 paper.
claims.quote: To address the expression and function of Hoxb13, the 5' most Hox gene in the HoxB cluster, we have generated mice with loss-of-function and beta-galactosidase reporter insertion alleles of this gene.

claims.claim: A peer-reviewed multi-species benchmark of splicing-variant prediction explicitly includes chicken (Gallus gallus) alongside human, rat and pig — making it, as of mid-2026, one of the very few published evaluations of genomic foundation models on an avian genome. It evaluated 10 methods: four task-specific models (SpliceAI, Pangolin, MMSplice, SpliceTransformer) and six genomic foundation models (DNABERT-2, Evo 2, Nucleotide Transformer, Genos, SpliceBERT, AlphaGenome). Note the scope limit: this is splicing-variant effect, NOT cis-regulatory/enhancer prediction, so it does not directly validate GFMs for the avian enhancer work the research question needs.
claims.quote: The study systematically evaluated 10 state-of-the-art approaches: four task-specific deep learning models (SpliceAI, Pangolin, MMSplice, SpliceTransformer) and six genomic foundation models (DNABERT-2, Evo 2, Nucleotide Transformer, Genos, SpliceBERT, AlphaGenome). The benchmark covered five species total: humans (two datasets) and three non-human vertebrates—rat, pig, and chicken.

claims.claim: Human-trained task-specific splicing models lose 21–33% AUROC when transferred to non-human species, quantifying the human-to-non-mammal transfer penalty. This is the direct empirical analogue of the mouse-to-bird transfer weakness flagged elsewhere in the research question: models trained on one clade do not transfer cleanly to birds without adaptation.
claims.quote: a substantial cross-species performance decrease (~21%–33% in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve - AUROC) using task-specific models from human to non-human species datasets.

claims.claim: Off-the-shelf zero-shot genomic foundation models are unreliable on this task: Nucleotide Transformer and SpliceBERT performed at essentially chance level (AUROC 0.5073 and 0.5163), while Evo 2 reached only 0.7089. This is a direct caution against using Evo 2 or Nucleotide Transformer zero-shot to score candidate avian regulatory variants — a single benchmark on splicing, so it should not be over-generalized, but it is the only quantitative avian-inclusive datapoint available.
claims.quote: near-random prediction performance with an AUROC of 0.5073 and 0.5163, respectively ... Evo 2: achieved an AUROC of 0.7089

This is the key methodological caveat for any claim that a developmental gene was lost in the avian stem lineage.

claims.claim: The false-loss signal has a specific, predictable genomic cause: absent genes cluster in centromeres, telomeres, acrocentric chromosomes and GC-extreme microchromosomes that short-read and earlier long-read assemblies could not reconstruct, so genes drop out in contiguous blocks. Any avian gene-loss or conserved-non-coding-element-loss claim must therefore be checked against assembly coverage of those regions before being accepted.
claims.quote: the missing genes are concentrated mainly in the centromeres, telomeres, acrocentric chromosomes, and microchromosomes, which are difficult to assemble ... suggesting that the reason for the absence of genes could not be found previously because of the difficulty in assembling certain highly heterochromatic microchromosomes completely, resulting in these adjacent gene blocks being missing in a block manner.

claims.quote: 33 Mb of new sequences

claims.claim: TNFA is a concrete worked example of a gene long treated as absent in birds that is in fact present and annotatable once the GC-rich microchromosome (Chr16) region is assembled — including in duck, where it had never been annotated before this work.

claims.claim: In Gallus gallus the pygostyle is formed POSTNATALLY by fusion of already-formed distal caudal vertebrae and remodeling of their intervertebral discs, proceeding distal-to-proximal after hatching — i.e. it is a separate developmental module from any embryonic tail-bud shortening event, and cannot be treated as evidence about caudal somite elimination.
claims.quote: Vertebral development continues near birth/hatching with a series of bone fusion events, including fusion of the neural arch components and fusion of the neural arches to the centra to form individual vertebrae... Because neighboring vertebral fusion occurs postnatally, after the IVDs and bony vertebrae have already formed, the ankylosis process requires the dismantling and remodeling of the discs to bone. ... Pygostyle formation entails remodeling of IVDs followed by bone formation in successive posthatching events that occur in the distal to proximal direction

claims.claim: The programmed cell death that clears avian pygostyle disc tissue is necroptosis (RIPK3/MLKL, TLR3/TLR4 upregulated), NOT classical caspase-dependent apoptosis; RIPK3 protein was 1.5-fold up in fusing vs free discs and RNAseq showed 12.3-fold RIPK3 mRNA upregulation. This is a distinct cell-death modality from the apoptosis usually invoked for tail-bud regression.
claims.quote: RIPK3 and MLKL upregulation indicates necroptosis, which likely accounts for the cell death we observed in fibroconnective tissue and AF cartilage. Toll-like receptors TLR3 and TLR4, upstream inducers of necroptosis in mammals (39), were also up-regulated. ... Accordingly, the caspase-specific cascade typical of classic apoptosis is not observed in our RNAseq data.

claims.claim: Pygostyle vertebral fusion is causally dependent on sterile inflammation: oral prednisolone from 3 to 8 weeks posthatch blocked fusion of the distalmost pygostyle IVD in 8 of 14 treated birds (57%), versus 100% fusion in untreated controls from 6 weeks onward — but the control group is n=8 total (2 at 6 wk, 2 at 7 wk, 4 at 8 wk), so this is a single non-replicated, small-n functional result.
claims.quote: Substantiating our hypothesis that inflammation drives pygostyle fusion, 57% (8 out of 14 total) of prednisolone-treated birds at the 8-wk timepoint failed to fuse their distalmost pygostyle IVD, compared to 100% fusion from 6 wk onward in the untreated controls (n = 2 at 6 wk, n = 2 at 7 wk, and n = 4 at 8 wk)

claims.claim: The avian caudal region retains the plesiomorphic (ancestral amniote) intervertebral disc developmental program, including true notochord-derived nucleus pulposus structures — found in both galliform (chicken) and paleognath (emu) tails — contradicting prior literature that birds lack NPs. This argues the avian tail program is retained rather than lost, i.e. tail reduction is unlikely to be a case of ancestral-program gene loss.
claims.quote: Similar to NP formation in mammals, we found that the notochord in avian tails fragments and its remnants become the central disc NP... The discovery of NP structures in avian tails has further implications for the evolution of the avian body plan, suggesting that the tail retains the plesiomorphic developmental program, and subsequent departures from that program occurred in more anterior axial regions.

claims.claim: Comparative axial fusion counts: Archaeopteryx had 4-6 fused sacral vertebrae, whereas Gallus gallus has 23-24 fused vertebrae distributed across notarium, synsacrum and pygostyle. (Note: these are FUSED-vertebra counts, not total caudal somite counts, and are stated from a figure adapted from ref. 9, not measured in this study.)
claims.quote: Archaeopteryx had 4 to 6 fused vertebrae in its sacrum. Bottom, diagram of the G. gallus spinal column, anterior to the Left. The chicken has 23 to 24 combined fused vertebrae in its axial column in the notarium, synsacrum, and pygostyle compound structures.

claims.claim: Pan et al. 2023 produced the most comprehensive chicken cis-regulatory atlas to date — 1.57 million regulatory elements in 15 ChromHMM chromatin states, ~1.2 million predicted enhancer-gene pairs and 7,662 super-enhancers — built from 377 ChIP-seq (H3K4me3/H3K4me1/H3K27ac/H3K27me3/CTCF), ATAC-seq, DNase-seq, RRBS, RNA-seq and Hi-C datasets. This is the resource that exists for avian enhancer identification, and it is bulk (no single-cell).
claims.quote: Here, we systematically identified and characterized regulatory elements in the chicken genome by integrating 377 genome-wide sequencing datasets from 23 adult tissues. In total, we annotated 1.57 million regulatory elements, representing 15 distinct chromatin states, and predicted about 1.2 million enhancer-gene pairs and 7662 super-enhancers.

claims.claim: The atlas is ADULT-ONLY and does not contain any embryonic, tailbud, somite or presomitic mesoderm sample: all 23 tissues came from four birds (21 tissues from two 20-week-old males, shell gland from two 20-week-old females, bursa from 3-week-old birds). Therefore it cannot be used directly to identify caudal/axial-elongation enhancers active at HH stages of avian tail-bud regression — any such use requires new embryonic ATAC/ChIP data, not this resource.
claims.quote: A total of 21 tissues were collected from two male birds (20 weeks of age) as in our previous report ( 12 , 45 ), including cortex, hypothalamus, cerebellum, testis, muscle, heart, adipose, kidney, spleen, bone marrow, lung, trachea, thymus, liver, proventriculus, gizzard, duodenum, jejunum, ileum, colon, and cecum. Shell glands were collected from two female birds at 20 weeks of age. Bursa tissues were collected from four birds of two highly inbred lines (two for each line) at 3 weeks of age

claims.claim: All coordinates in the atlas are on galGal6 (GRCg6a) with Ensembl v100 annotation, NOT the current GRCg7b/bGalGal1.mat broiler reference — so any genomic coordinate taken from this resource must be lifted over before being used with a current assembly or with models trained on newer chicken references.
claims.quote: Briefly, the galGal6 genome assembly and Ensembl genome annotation (v100) have been used as reference.

claims.claim: No chicken enhancer in this atlas was functionally validated experimentally; 'validation' was an in-silico enrichment test against the VISTA database of enhancers validated in humans and mice, from which the authors infer only 'potential conservation' across humans, mice and birds. The atlas is therefore a prediction set, not a set of proven avian enhancers.
claims.quote: To validate enhancers predicted in our study in silico, we queried the VISTA database ( 17 ), which contains information on functionally validated enhancers in humans and mice. As expected, we found that strong (EnhA) and medium (EnhAme) enhancers demonstrated higher enrichments in the VISTA enhancers than the other types of enhancers ( Fig. 2H ). ... These findings not only provided additional evidence for the functionality of enhancers identified in our study but also suggested potential conservation of some enhancers among humans, mice, and birds.

claims.claim: Enhancer-to-target-gene assignment in the atlas is statistical and low-resolution: pairs were inferred by correlating H3K27ac signal with gene expression inside predicted CTCF loops, giving a median enhancer-gene distance of ~249 kb, 18 enhancers per gene and 3 target genes per enhancer. Any candidate regulatory target picked from this resource is a correlational hypothesis, not a mapped enhancer-promoter link.
claims.quote: To predict the target gene(s) for each enhancer, we correlated the signal intensity of H3K27ac and the expression level of genes within the same predicted CTCF loop region (see Materials and Methods). In total, we obtained ~1.2 million enhancer-gene pairs with a median distance of 249,346 bp across all tissues. On average, each gene was linked to 18 enhancers, whereas each enhancer targeted three genes

claims.claim: Seki et al. identified 265,984 avian-specific highly conserved elements (ASHCEs) from a 48-bird + 9-outgroup whole-genome alignment; >99% are non-coding, they total ~11 Mbp (~1% of the avian genome), and their substitution rate (~0.0004 subs/site/Myr) is ~5-fold below the genome average. This is a gain of lineage-specific constraint in non-coding DNA, not sequence loss — directly relevant to whether avian traits arise from regulatory rewiring rather than gene loss.
claims.quote: In total, our analysis predicted 265,984 ASHCEs (≥20 bp), representing nearly 1% of the avian genome (ca. 11 Mbp in total, Supplementary Table 3). These ASHCEs had an extremely low substitution rate (about 0.0004 substitutions per site per million years, Supplementary Table 7), ∼fivefold lower than the whole-genome average.

claims.claim: The paper's framing premise is that birds lost thousands of protein-coding genes and carry fewer paralogues per gene family than other vertebrates, and the authors explicitly infer from this that protein-coding innovation was NOT a major driver of the dinosaur-to-bird transition, favouring cis-regulatory change instead. Note this is an inference from gene-family counts, not a test of any specific caudal/axial locus.
claims.quote: birds have furthermore lost thousands of the protein-coding genes in their common ancestors after the split from other reptiles10,11. By applying gene family clustering analyses across multiple genomes representing birds, mammals, fishes and other reptiles, we found that bird genomes have on average a relatively lower number of paralogous copies within protein-coding gene families than other vertebrates (Fig. 1a). This result implies that innovation of protein-coding genes might not play a large role in the processes underlying the transitions from dinosaur to the bird lineage.

claims.claim: ASHCEs are defined by two operationally distinct patterns — Type I has no alignable orthologue in any non-avian outgroup (including Alligator mississippiensis), Type II has an orthologue that evolves significantly faster in outgroups (phyloP FDR-corrected P<0.01 against alligator alone, three non-avian reptiles, and nine vertebrates). So the avian stem lineage signal reported here is acquired avian constraint, not avian-accelerated relaxation of ancestral elements; the study does not scan for CNE loss in birds.
claims.quote: We then determined which of these HCEs had either no orthologues in non-avian outgroups (Type I), or whose orthologues exhibit significantly higher substitution rates among outgroups (Type II; Fig. 1b). The genomic regions displaying such unique conservation pattern among birds are subsequently defined as avian-specific HCEs (ASHCEs).

claims.claim: A single 284 bp ASHCE in intron 8 of Sim1 was functionally validated as an enhancer both by in ovo electroporation into the chicken HH13-14 forelimb field and by hsp68-LacZ transgenic mice, establishing a worked precedent that one avian-specific non-coding element can account for an avian-specific expression domain. Caveat: the deletion-negative construct and mouse transgenics are single-locus reporter assays, not endogenous knockouts.
claims.quote: To elucidate whether the Sim1-associated ASHCE serves as a cis-regulatory element responsible for avian-specific expression, we conducted reporter assays using two different methods for one of the Sim1-associated ASHCEs, that is 284 bp long and is located at the eighth intron of Sim1 (Fig. 5a).

claims.claim: The only tail-related result is Sim1 expression flanking the developing rectrices (tail flight feathers) in chicken at HH28-HH35, absent from the gecko tail tip; the ASHCE is dated to ~144.0 ± 26.6 Myr ago. The paper reports nothing on caudal somite number, pygostyle formation, tail-bud apoptosis, or axial-termination genes (HOX13, TBXT/Brachyury, GDF11, CDX, LIN28), and its functional follow-up (ChIP-seq, in situ screen of 100 top ASHCE genes) is limb- and feather-focused, with the limb-development ASHCE genes named being FMN1, GLI3, LEF1, MEOX2 and PRRX1. This source therefore does NOT supply evidence on avian tail reduction per se.
claims.quote: we found that Sim1 was expressed in the both lateral sides of the tail and the region around the cloaca at HH28 chicken embryo (Fig. 6b). At HH32, the buds of flight feathers were observed along the expression of Sim1 nearby the posterior tip of the tail (Fig. 6c), and its expression was maintained till HH35 (Fig. 6d).

claims.claim: The hominoid tail-loss lesion is a single non-coding insertion acting through RNA structure, not a coding change: an AluY inserted into intron 6 of TBXT pairs with an inverted, simian-shared AluSx1 in intron 5, forming an exon-flanking inverted repeat that traps exon 6 in a stem-loop and produces a hominoid-specific TBXT(delta-exon6) splice isoform. Xia et al. 2024, Nature 626:1042-1048, doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07095-8.
claims.quote: We demonstrate that this Alu element-inserted into an intron of the TBXT gene-pairs with a neighbouring ancestral Alu element encoded in the reverse genomic orientation and leads to a hominoid-specific alternative splicing event.

claims.claim: A genome-wide hominoid-specific variant screen across 140 tail-development genes (plus 10 kb flanks) found NO causal protein-coding variant - 85,064 SNVs, 5,533 deletions and 13,820 insertions were hominoid-specific, and the nine protein-altering candidates were deprioritized - establishing that this validated tail-shortening precedent is a regulatory/splicing lesion rather than gene loss or pseudogenization. Note the comparative genomics rests on older assemblies (hg38, panTro5, gorGor5, panPan2, ponAbe2, nomLeu3, macNem1, calJac3; Ensembl 109, MGI Feb 2023), pre-dating current T2T primate assemblies.
claims.quote: Failing to detect candidate variants in the coding regions of this gene set, we expanded the search in two ways: (1) adding 109 genes for which mutation in their mouse orthologues includes tail-reduction phenotypes annotated in the MGI as 'vestigial tail' or 'short tail'; and (2) systematically screening for hominoid-specific variants in the entire gene region and their 10 kb upstream and downstream sequences

claims.claim: The phenotype was demonstrated only in MOUSE, not in any primate or non-mammalian model, and is dosage-dependent and incompletely penetrant: Tbxt exon-6-deleted heterozygotes showed tail phenotypes in 21 of 63 animals versus 0 of 35 wild-type littermates, while compound heterozygotes with higher delta-exon6 abundance showed complete tail absence in 19 of 19. Tail length tracks the ratio of delta-exon6 to full-length transcript in the E10.5 tailbud, not the presence of the insertion per se - the Alu-pair insertion mouse itself was declared inconclusive because it expressed too little of the isoform in the tailbud.
claims.quote: Specifically, 21 out of the 63 heterozygous mice showed tail phenotypes, whereas none of their 35 wild-type littermates showed phenotypes

claims.claim: The design-constraint cost is real but the evidence for it is thin: homozygous Tbxt(delta-exon6) mice were non-viable, arresting at about E9 or dying at birth with spinal cord malformations, and the neural-tube-defect claim rests on individual dead pups (one delta-exon6 homozygote plus one pup of the other line) rather than a scored incidence across a cohort - a single-study, low-n observation that should not be quoted as a quantified NTD rate.
claims.quote: Moreover, mice expressing the exon-skipped Tbxt isoform develop neural tube defects, a condition that affects approximately 1 in 1,000 neonates in humans.

claims.claim: The authors explicitly argue that reverting the causal insertion would NOT be expected to restore the ancestral tail, because additional genetic changes are likely to have accumulated to stabilize the no-tail state - a direct caution against treating a single identified regulatory lesion as a sufficient in-silico reversal target in any atavism design, avian included.
claims.quote: Such a possible set of genetic events suggest that a change to the AluY element in modern hominoids would be unlikely to result in the reappearance of the tail.

claims.claim: In Gallus gallus the pygostyle is NOT formed embryonically: the four core pygostyle vertebrae are still separate and ossified at 8 days post-hatch, fusion proceeds distal-to-proximal, and is complete only at ~5 months of age (confirmed by microCT at 7-8 weeks vs 1.5 years). Prior reports of embryonic pygostyle fusion are attributed to a staining artifact (alcian blue stains intervertebral disc and vertebral cartilage identically). NOTE: the paper is entirely skeletal/histological ontogeny — it contains no discussion whatsoever of somites, tail-bud apoptosis, programmed cell death, or Hamburger-Hamilton staging of axial termination (zero hits for 'somite', 'apoptosis', 'cell death' in the full text).
claims.quote: While some studies have suggested that pygostyle fusion (and hence formation) occurs during embryonic cartilage development9,16,17, closer examination shows that pygostyle vertebrae in the chicken do not fuse until post hatching. ... At eight days post-hatching, all four core pygostyle vertebrae are separate and distinct. By five months of age, the core pygostyle vertebrae are fully fused. Pygostyle formation in the chicken, therefore, occurs as a post-hatch event between ossified vertebrae.

claims.claim: The ONLY genetic/developmental mechanism the paper invokes for the long- to short-tailed transition is extrapolated from mouse mutants, not measured in birds: mouse mutations that fuse caudal vertebrae also usually reduce caudal vertebral number, with pleiotropic axial and limb fusions, which the authors use to argue the avian short tail could have arisen from few Cretaceous mutations. This is an explicit mouse-to-bird transfer with no chicken molecular data in this paper — exactly the weak link to flag.
claims.quote: Earlier analyses of vertebrate mutations indicated that at least some pygostylian features could have arisen from very few mutations. These analyses were conducted in mice, and indicated that mutations that cause tail vertebrae to fuse also usually decrease the number of caudal vertebrae9. Additional pleiotropic effects of tail shortening and tail fusing mutations include more extensive vertebral fusion along the axial column, as well as peripheral fusions in the limbs, akin to the bone fusions observed in Pygostylia birds9.

claims.claim: The number of caudal vertebrae incorporated into the pygostyle is not fixed across birds: the maximum among the extant taxa surveyed was five (Humboldt penguin), whereas microCT of a subadult Confuciusornis sanctus pygostyle (NGMC 98-8-2) indicates ~eight ankylosed vertebrae, with a similar estimate for juvenile enantiornithine IVPP V15664. Relative pygostyle/femur length shows confuciusornithids and enantiornithines exceeded all other measured groups.
claims.quote: MicroCT scanning of a Confuciusornis sanctus pygostyle (NGMC 98-8-2;18) indicates that in this subadult, approximately eight vertebrae ankylosed into the pygostyle, evident by the number of unfused neural arch components ... In the extant birds analyzed in this study, the greatest number of pygostyle vertebrae was five, estimated for the Humboldt penguin

claims.claim: Distal caudal fusion and reduced caudal vertebral count are correlated outside Aves as well: Caudipteryx, a non-avian oviraptorosaur, had a distally fused tail and fewer caudal vertebrae than oviraptorosaurs lacking distal fusion; Pteranodon, a short-tailed pterodactyloid, is likewise described as distally fused. The authors use this to argue tail shortening and caudal fusion are mechanistically linked traits.
claims.quote: The tail of Pteranodon, a short-tailed pterodactyloid, has been described as distally fused12, reinforcing a potential link between tail shortening and caudal vertebral fusion. Caudipteryx, a non-avian oviraptorosaur, also had a distally fused tail with fewer caudal vertebrae than other oviraptorosaurs lacking distal fusion13.

claims.claim: Because pygostyle fusion is post-hatching, the absence of a pygostyle in a juvenile Mesozoic specimen is not evidence of a transitional long-to-short-tail morphology: Zhongornis haoae (125 Ma, Yixian) is a juvenile and cannot be identified as an intermediate, and the 99 Ma amber-embedded coelurosaur tail — called non-avian partly on absence of vertebral processes and a ventral furrow — is reinterpreted as possibly avian, since chicken parapophyses are still uncalcified at E19 and a ventral caudal furrow is a common extant avian trait.
claims.quote: This specimen, however, is a juvenile, and its pygostyle may not yet have fused in ontogeny. Until a full-grown specimen is discovered, to indicate whether adults of this species had unfused pygostyle vertebrae, the Zhongornis haoae holotype cannot be definitively identified as an intermediate in the long- to short-tailed transition.

claims.claim: Programmed cell death does NOT eliminate distal caudal somites in the chicken tail. TUNEL at E4–E7 (HH~22–31) shows apoptosis confined to residual tailbud mesenchyme and ventrolateral dermomyotome, explicitly excluded from somite domains; the authors conclude somite number stays constant through chick tail development. This directly refutes the 'distal somites are resorbed' model of avian tail reduction. CAVEAT: single study, qualitative TUNEL with no quantification or n reported, chicken only; it does however agree with prior independent work (Schoenwolf 1981; Hirata & Hall 2000; Miller & Briglin 1996; Sanders 1997).
claims.quote: TUNEL assays performed at E4 through E7 stages confirm that apoptosis does not affect terminal somites, in agreement with other studies. Robust cell death is only observed in the remnant of the tailbud mesenchyme (especially at E4 to E5), and in the ventrolateral dermomyotome... That cell death occurs primarily outside of somite domains supports the notion that resorption of somites does not occur. [...] Combined with the lack of apoptosis, the number of somites therefore remains constant in chicken tail development.

claims.claim: Concrete caudal-element counts for the bird-vs-crocodilian-vs-stem-bird comparison: chicken and quail have 9 caudal vertebrae (5 free + 4 pygostyle), rock dove 9–10 (5–6 free + 4 pygostyle), emu 8 (5 free + 3 pygostyle); American alligator and brown anole each have ~40 caudal vertebrae; Archaeopteryx had >20. The avian pygostyle domain in Gallus is therefore the distalmost 4 pre-vertebrae. CAVEAT: emu counts are the authors' own observations from one museum specimen (MOR 186) plus three post-hatch carcasses — small, non-replicated sample; alligator/anole counts are cited from prior literature.
claims.quote: The avian species examined have similar caudal vertebrae counts; nine in the chicken and quail (5 free vertebrae and 4 pygostyle vertebrae; our observations), nine to ten in the rock dove (5 to 6 free vertebrae and 4 pygostyle vertebrae and our observations), and eight in the emu (5 free vertebrae and three pygostyle vertebrae... Pre-hatching developmental analysis was then performed in alligator and brown anole (both have approximately 40 caudal vertebrae) [...] Archaeopteryx , the earliest known bird, sported a long, reptilian-like tail with greater than 20 caudal vertebrae

claims.claim: The avian distal-tail developmental program is NOT universal across birds: in the paleognath emu, DRGs, sympathetic ganglia and spinal nerve roots form all the way to the distalmost sclerotome and through the pygostyle region at the HH36-equivalent stage, whereas chicken, Chinese painted quail and rock dove (all neognaths) lack DRG formation in the distalmost ~4 pre-vertebrae. Sclerotome A/P polarity (PNA staining) likewise differs: diffuse/absent in the neognath pygostyle region, but staining centra and neural arches in emu. This means any 'reverse the avian tail' design premised on a single pan-avian mechanism is wrong at the outset. CAVEAT: emu evidence rests on very few embryos from one supplier, one HH36-equivalent stage, and no other paleognath was tested embryologically — the authors themselves call for more taxa.
claims.quote: However, in the paleognathous emu, the neognathous pattern was not observed, such that spinal nerve development extends through the pygostyle region. [...] Unlike chicken, dove, and quail, DRGs (arrowheads) and sympathetic ganglia (arrows) form in the pygostyle, to the very distal end of the tail. [...] The disparate emu distal spinal nerve development indicates that the process of axial peripheral nervous system termination is not universal in avians.

claims.claim: Absence of spinal nerve development at the extreme tail tip is the ANCESTRAL archosaur/diapsid condition, not an avian novelty: American alligator embryos (stages 13, 20, 23, 26) lack spinal root development alongside the six distalmost sclerotomes, with the most distal DRG between the 6th and 7th vertebrae from the tail end, and brown anole (Anolis sagrei, stage 10) shows the same six-sclerotome gap. Long-tailed reptiles therefore already truncate the distal PNS, so distal-PNS truncation cannot be the causal lesion that shortened the avian tail. CAVEAT: this is a single non-replicated study; alligator and anole n are not stated, and the inference that emu is derived rather than basal is explicitly framed by the authors as hypothesis ('several possible scenarios'), including the unconventional claim of an independent paleognath long-tailed ancestor.
claims.quote: Surprisingly, like chicken, rock dove and quail (but unlike emu), alligator embryos lack distal spinal nerve development... Spinal root development was absent in the six distal sclerotomes at the tail tip. [...] Like alligator, chicken, rock dove and quail, brown anole embryos lack spinal nerve formation at the tail tip; no spinal nerve development was observed alongside their distalmost six sclerotomes. From these data, we hypothesize that the ancestral configuration is an absence of spinal nerve development at the distalmost end of the tail.

claims.claim: Where a molecular cause for distal chick tail phenotypes is invoked, it is REGULATORY (altered expression levels/domains) rather than gene loss: the failure of DRG formation in the distal chick tail is attributed to maintained Noggin expression with concomitant loss of Bmp4 and Wnt1 expression, plus a sclerotome A/P polarity deficit (absent PNA target blocking neural crest delamination), with distal neural crest cells intrinsically restricted to Schwann/glial rather than neuronal fates. The paper also cites the rumpless Araucana chicken as an IRX1/IRX2 gain-of-function mutation disrupting axis elongation. Nowhere does the paper report pseudogenization, gene loss, or conserved-non-coding-element loss in the avian caudal program. CAVEAT: the Noggin/Bmp4/Wnt1 attribution is cited from a prior study (ref. 50), not generated here; the authors state 'multiple processes are involved', so no single-lesion target is identified.
claims.quote: a lack of DRG formation in the distal tail has been observed and was found to be at least partly attributed to maintained expression of Noggin and concomitant loss of Bmp4 and Wnt1. Neural crest cells form in reduced numbers the more posterior... but are also unable to delaminate, possibly due to the lack of the PNA target, and are depleted by apoptosis. Intrinsic to the neural crest cells from this axial level, the cells are only capable of differentiation to Schwann cells and glia, not to neurons. These results, in combination with compromised sclerotome polarity, show that multiple processes are involved that prevent distal spinal nerve formation in the chicken.

claims.claim: In a genome-wide test across 79 bird genomes for a convergent skeletal-reduction trait (short tarsus), the signal was entirely regulatory: 14,422 conserved non-exonic elements showed convergent acceleration, while 9,854 one-to-one protein-coding orthologs showed NO convergent positive selection. This is a direct empirical precedent that avian skeletal reduction can be a cis-regulatory problem rather than a gene-loss/coding problem — but note the trait is tarsus (hindlimb) length; the paper analyzes no axial, caudal, vertebral or pygostyle trait, and the words tail, caudal, pygostyle, TBXT and GDF11 do not appear anywhere in it.
claims.quote: Using multiple approaches, we failed to find evidence of convergent evolution of protein coding sequences in short-tarsus focal clades. We recovered 9854 one-to-one orthologous loci using TOGA with subsequent filtering for quality and number of taxa. Using aBS-REL [], a branch-site-based test of selection that accounted for synonymous rate variation [], we identify 1534 (15.6%) genes with selection in least one short-tarsus focal clade. ... Fisher's exact tests comparing genes under selection in the focal group and in representative outgroups showed no evidence of convergence for any pairwise, three-way, or four-way comparisons.

claims.claim: The paper publishes a reusable, currently-assembled avian regulatory resource: 932,467 avian conserved non-exonic elements built from a ProgressiveCactus whole-genome alignment of 79 bird assemblies and mapped onto the chicken assembly galGal7b (RefSeq GCF_016699485.2), validated against the 363-species avian alignment. Acceleration was tested with PhyloAcc-ST using separate neutral models for macrochromosomes, microchromosomes and the Z. This is an off-the-shelf pipeline and coordinate system that could be re-targeted to caudal/axial loci; it also means any older element set (galGal4/galGal5-based) needs liftover, which the authors themselves had to perform.
claims.quote: All five sets of conserved elements were mapped to the chicken assembly(Refseq Accession: GCF_016699485.2; subsequently referred to as galGal7b), resulting in a total of 1,117,392 elements with a mean substitution rate of 38% of the neutral rate ... leaving a final set of 932,467 conserved elements (median length 71 bp, mean length 122 bp, maximum length 4620 bp)

claims.claim: A chicken cis-regulatory atlas usable for enhancer identification exists and was used here: ATAC-seq peaks from chicken (and emu) hindlimb at Hamburger-Hamilton stage HH18. 4,151 of 7,948 accelerated elements (52.2%) overlapped chicken ATAC-seq peaks, 1,575 of them open in chicken hindlimb at HH18. Cross-species chromatin state was imputed with TACIT, a convolutional-neural-network classifier trained on the chicken and emu HH18 peaks — an actually-deployed machine-learning method validated on avian genomes, unlike genomic language models.
claims.quote: Of the 7948 accelerated elements in the short-tarsus broad dataset, 4151 (52.2%) overlapped chicken ATAC-seq peaks, of which 1575 were open in chicken hindlimbs at HH18 stage, whereas in the short-tarsus-specific dataset, 216 of the 403 elements (53.5%) overlapped ATAC-seq peaks with 102 elements open in hindlimbs at HH18 stage.

claims.claim: Convergently accelerated elements were recovered near Hox clusters (including an a9-a11 cluster region), but the authors state explicitly that element-to-gene assignment inside Hox clusters is NOT resolvable by this method because Hox genes are tightly clustered near many conserved elements. This is a hard design constraint for any in-silico plan that would target a specific HOX13 paralog enhancer in chicken: proximity-based assignment cannot name the target gene.
claims.quote: Hox genes, however, tend to be clustered together in the genome [] near multiple conserved elements, which prevents us from identifying specific Hox genes that are associated with a particular element.

claims.claim: Sequence acceleration of a conserved element is not by itself evidence of adaptive regulatory change: PhyloAcc cannot distinguish positive selection from loss of constraint, and when the authors applied a noncoding McDonald-Kreitman test using population resequencing data only 2.04% of accelerated elements in bulbuls (18 elements) and 4.77% in swallows (41 elements) showed positive selection. Any claim that an 'avian-accelerated regulatory element' caused a phenotype therefore requires population-genetic or functional follow-up, not acceleration alone.
claims.quote: PhyloAcc detects elements where one or more branches show a shift in conservation state (e.g., from conserved to non-conserved), but by itself cannot determine whether this shift in conservation is driven by positive selection or loss of constraint. Although on average, we find that the substitution rate in accelerated branches is greater than the neutral rate, mutational processes such as GC-biased gene convergence can drive substitution rates in excess of the neutral rate for unconstrained sequence in the absence of positive selection

claims.claim: Rashid et al. give concrete caudal vertebral counts across the transition: Archaeopteryx 20-23, Jeholornis 22, Sapeornis the first bird with only 6-7 free caudals plus an elongated pygostyle, and modern chicken 5-6 free caudal vertebrae plus a pygostyle formed by fusion of the final 5-6 somites. No Alligator count is given anywhere in the paper, and no Caudipteryx count is given (only that oviraptorosaurs had shorter tails, and Epidexipteryx had 16 caudals). Note the pygostyle count is stated as a fusion of 'somites', not vertebrae, which is a loose usage.
claims.quote: Extending beyond the synsacrum, the mature tail in the chick consists of 5 to 6 free caudal vertebrae (there are 5 to 8 free caudal vertebrae among birds in general) and the pygostyle (a fusion of the final 5 to 6 somites).

claims.claim: In Gallus gallus the segmentation clock decelerates rather than stopping abruptly: the first 45 somite pairs form at ~90 min each, the final 5-8 caudal somites (the pygostyle precursors) at ~150 min each; WNT3A is highly expressed in tail mesenchyme up to HH21 and is downregulated between HH22 and HH25, with RALDH2 (ALDH1A2) upregulated in chick tail mesenchyme as the proposed cause of WNT3A/FGF8 downregulation. The chick tail reaches its maximum somite number by E5. These are the specific HH stages and cell-biological landmarks for avian axial termination.
claims.quote: In the chick, the first 45 pairs of somites take 90 minutes each to form; thereafter, the segmentation clock slows such that the final 5 to 8 caudal somites (predecessors of the pygostyle) take 150 minutes to form []. One likely candidate for this deceleration is WNT3a. While somitogenesis is robustly proceeding, up to HH (Hamburger Hamilton []) stage 21, WNT3a is highly expressed in the tail mesenchyme, but as somite addition and the need for PSM nears its close, WNT3a is gradually downregulated between HH22 and HH25 [].

claims.claim: The review explicitly REJECTS the idea that distal caudal somites are eliminated primarily by programmed cell death. Apoptosis in the tail bud is described as contributing but neither sufficient nor solitary, and the authors cite two disconfirming observations: substantial mesenchymal cell death occurs while the tail is still robustly extending, and apoptosis has been pharmacologically/genetically inhibited in several vertebrates without producing longer tails. Depletion of the chordoneural hinge progenitor pool via reduced cell division, neuroblast cell-cycle exit, and PSM becoming unresponsive is presented as the dominant mechanism instead. This directly contradicts the common secondhand claim that the avian tail is 'apoptotically removed'.
claims.quote: The concept that apoptosis plays a contributing but not solitary role in tail cessation is further substantiated by the fact that significant mesenchyme cell death occurs even while the tail is robustly extending [], and apoptosis has been inhibited in different vertebrates, but longer tails have not been documented [].

claims.claim: As of 2014 no experimental manipulation in any bird had ever produced a longer tail or an increased number of caudal somites/vertebrae — including a specific failed attempt (Noggin inhibition in chick tail, which upregulated neural crest markers but added no somites). The only known spontaneous avian axial-truncation mutation is the rumpless Araucana chicken, attributed to gain-of-function of Irx1/Irx2, in which the most caudal somites are never generated and the pygostyle never forms (heterozygotes retain 2-4 irregularly fused caudal elements). Critically for mouse-to-bird transfer, the authors flag that Irx1 or Irx2 loss-of-function in mouse causes neither posterior truncation nor fused vertebrae. In mouse, only 2 of 159 tail mutants (Hoxb13 KO, +2 caudal vertebrae; Slx4) lengthen the tail at all. This is the hard design constraint on any in-silico 'tail restoration' plan: the perturbation space is overwhelmingly one-directional toward shortening.
claims.quote: To our knowledge, no manipulations in the bird have resulted in longer tails with increased numbers of caudal somites/vertebrae. One study attempted to extend neural crest in chick embryo tails by inhibiting Noggin []. While certain neural crest markers were indeed upregulated at the end of the tail, additional somites were not added and tail length remained unchanged.

claims.claim: The review presents NO evidence of gene loss, pseudogenization, or conserved-non-coding-element loss in the avian axial/caudal program. It invokes gene inactivation only for the separate case of tooth/enamel loss, and frames avian tail reduction instead as an unidentified coding or cis-regulatory mutation in axial-extension genes (most likely Notch/Wnt somite-segmentation genes), explicitly conceding the causal mutation is unknown and the single-mutation scenario is a hypothesis, not a finding. This means that on the evidence in this review, tail reduction and tooth loss are NOT the same class of problem: teeth have documented pseudogenes, the tail does not.
claims.quote: We have no way of knowing at this point, of course, what or how many mutations occurred in early bird evolution, or even which was the true basal ancestor that sustained the initial mutations. Despite the many caveats with this approach, however, our analyses of genetic and fossil evidence suggest the possibility that a single mutation could have occurred in a paravian dinosaur, which both truncated its tail and fused its distal caudal vertebrae into a pygostyle.

- Chicken: "Extending beyond the synsacrum, the mature tail in the chick consists of 5 to 6 free caudal vertebrae ... and the pygostyle (a fusion of the final 5 to 6 somites)" — the supplied supporting quote is exact, and the claim's rendering of it is faithful.
- Epidexipteryx: "Its tail had only 16 caudal vertebrae with the distal ten tightly articulated" — matches "16 caudals".

input.summary: The avian tail was shortened by an unidentified change in the embryonic axial-extension program, and on the evidence retrieved here that change is regulatory-or-unknown, not gene loss: no source in this pass reports a single pseudogene, gene loss, or lost conserved non-coding element in the avian axial/caudal program, which puts tail reduction in a fundamentally different evidentiary class from avian tooth loss (where enamel/dentin pseudogenes are documented). Concretely, Gallus has ~9 caudal elements (5 free + 4 pygostyle) against ~40 in Alligator and >20 in Archaeopteryx, with Sapeornis the first bird at 6-7 free caudals plus pygostyle; the pygostyle itself is NOT an embryonic structure but a post-hatch ankylosis event completed at ~5 months, so it is a separate module from whatever reduced caudal somite number and cannot be cited as evidence about somite elimination. Programmed cell death in the chick tail bud is real but restricted to tail gut, primitive-streak remnant and ventral mesenchyme — the same 1996 source explicitly reports apoptosis markers absent from neural tube, notochord and somites — and later chick work places tailbud cell death downstream of rising retinoid signalling, concluding rather than triggering termination. Every molecular terminator of axial extension with real functional evidence (GDF11 trunk-to-tail switch, LIN28A/let-7 dosage controlling the caudal progenitor pool, CDX1/2/4 dosage, HOX13) is established in MOUSE ONLY; this pass found zero avian loss- or gain-of-function data for any of them, so the mouse-to-bird transfer is unvalidated at every node — and the one chicken-native genetic lesion (Araucana rumpless IRX1/IRX2 gain-of-function) is breed-specific, based on six sequenced birds, and never functionally validated. Sub-questions 3 (Xia 2024 TBXT/AluY), 5 (genomic language model validity on non-mammalian vertebrates, chicken PGC editing, chicken cis-regulatory atlases) and 6 (ethics/regulation) returned no surviving verified clai...
